The Hidden Cost of a Hit Product

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, between 2022 and 2025, Miu Miu was on fire.
  • Now, Miu Miu’s explosive sales growth has normalized, recording a 2.4% increase in Q1 2026, against a 60% increase the year prior, according to Prada Group’s most recent earnings.
  • The Miu Miu cropped jumper and mini skirt set as seen on influencer Caro Daur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, between 2022 and 2025, Miu Miu was on fire. Driven by a string of viral product releases including the ultra-low-rise micro-mini skirt, a New Balance 530 collaboration and its logo ballet flats, the label saw rapid growth. In 2024, revenue grew 93% on the previous year. And by the end of 2025, it accounted for 31% of Prada Group’s retail sales, up from 25% a year earlier.

Now, Miu Miu’s explosive sales growth has normalized, recording a 2.4% increase in Q1 2026, against a 60% increase the year prior, according to Prada Group’s most recent earnings. This slowed growth was expected: during the first-quarter earnings call, Prada Group CEO Andrea Guerra mentioned Miu Miu was dealing with a “disrupted environment, against the most challenging comparison base of the year”. In other words, Miu Miu did so well during its viral product peak that even a solid performance today looks like a slowdown (Miu Miu didn’t respond to request for comment).

The Miu Miu cropped jumper and mini skirt set as seen on influencer Caro Daur.

It has been revealed that this isn’t an isolated example. Elsewhere, Hermès – which had remained a bright spot post pandemic as other brands faltered – recently recorded slower-than-expected growth over the nine months ending September 30, 2026. Ready-to-wear and accessories were down 2.1% on the previous year, weighing on overall performance. CFO Éric du Halgouët told investors during the earnings call that the decline is partly due to a contraction in “high-volume” categories such as footwear and non-handbag accessories like belts. Alongside many footwear styles, this category includes the Hermès Oran sandal, which offers an entry point to the house for more aspirational consumers, retailing at around $900. Hermès declined to comment for this story.

Industry observers note that viral hit products are undeniably a boon for brands, both for revenue and relevance. But there’s a downside once their star inevitably fades: difficult comps. In a challenging macroeconomic environment, where brands are seeking new customers and growth, they must strike a balance between sales spikes driven by virality and long-term brand desirability.

Regardless of the brand, “a single hit can keep sales strong while hiding [softer] demand elsewhere and failing to attract the next generation,” says Jeanel Alvarado, founder and editor-in-chief of RetailBoss. “When demand slows, the brand must replace lost revenue and build fresh demand, with less money available to do either.”.

According to recent reports, sneakers are a key category for viral items. Alvarado highlights Balenciaga’s Demna-era Triple S sneaker as another hit piece that inflated brand sales after its release in 2017, before creating tough comparisons for the label once it fell out of fashion. “Its exaggerated silhouette connected luxury with the way people were dressing in everyday life,” she claims. “The challenge comes when demand for those few recognizable products becomes stronger than customers’ interest in the wider collection.” A year after the Triple S hit the market, Kering’s 2018 report praised the “continuing exceptional momentum of Balenciaga”.

The Balenciaga Triple S sneaker was first shown in the FW17 menswear collection.

Likewise, McQueen’s entry-level Oversized Sneaker represented 80% of brand revenues at its peak in the late 2010s, according to Kering CEO Luca de Meo, during Kering’s full year 2025 earnings call in February of this year. According to analysts at Bernstein, the house’s turnover fell from €850 million to €200 million between 2022 and 2025.

“When sales are under pressure, brands [can] double down on products customers already understand and can more easily justify buying,” indicates Alvarado. Across brands, popular products are backed up by sales data, and begin to take more rail space and marketing attention, delivering short-term and easy wins. “The short-term need to protect revenue then leaves fewer resources to build demand for alternatives. That is how a sensible buying decision becomes a longer-term dependence.”.

For brands, cashing in on a hit product makes immediate and obvious commercial sense. Done well, it welcomes upcoming consumers into the fold, offering a short-term sales increase and the opportunity to convert them into long-term fans. But problems may arise when the entry-level product is pumped out without being replaced by another hit once demand fades.

In a recent development, “A breakout, viral product can lift a brand quickly, but once it’s everywhere, it loses the exclusivity that made people want it,” says Katy Lubin, VP of brand and communications at Lyst. Ubiquity is a problem for luxury brands, in particular. “It’s hard to spend a lot of money on something and then see it everywhere,” adds Marissa Lepor, managing director of The Sage Group. “The more prevalent that a luxury item becomes, the core customer of the luxury brand is less interested in it. They feel like it’s everywhere, or they already have enough of them.” Nowadays, this is happening quicker than ever. The rise of short-form video means that trends come and go much faster.

Conner Ives’s viral vintage robe from his SS27 collection.

If an item is too visible, it also runs the risk of being duped by more accessible contemporary or high street players, quickening its trend half-life and further reducing its appeal to luxury consumers. While many luxury customers won’t be interested in a dupe, other potential buyers may be tempted by a cheaper alternative. “It can really amplify the conversation around those hero products, but maybe doesn’t scale as much with sales,” Lepor claims. “The person who’s coveting that luxury item might not end up buying it, they might end up buying something similar.”.

It has been revealed that one way to reduce reliance on a small number of items or categories is to reduce supply — something luxury houses have often employed. “Hermès and Rolex still sell less of their iconic products than their market would take,” says Luca Solca, managing director of luxury goods at Bernstein. For Hermès, its intricate leather goods production creates scarcity, rather than the brand holding back product, according to artistic director Pierre-Alexis Dumas, who told CBS’s 60 Minutes that “whatever we have, we put on the shelf, and it goes”, in 2024.

The Hermès Oran sandal seen on a guest at Berlin Fashion Week SS27.

Sources indicate that when supply stays below demand, hero products never become ubiquitous and the market remains unsaturated, even if the product goes viral. “There has to be a balance between what a brand is known for, what products get mass scale and how to keep the scarcity,” says Lepor, “so that when you invest in these luxury items, you feel unique.”.

Sources indicate that brands can avoid potential overreliance by using the exposure that comes with a popular item as an opportunity to introduce consumers to a wider brand universe. “It is good to have an iconic product that everybody wants, [but] it is better to follow-up with more products to build on this,” says Solca.

In a recent development, “If you have a few designs that become really popular, they become popular for a reason,” indicates Lepor. “It’s less figuring out why something went wrong, and more figuring out how to iterate upon it to do something like that again. Something I think is really important with the luxury world right now, is not just selling people one item, but getting them to covet the world of the brand.” Lepor points to Cartier’s Love bracelet, as well as the wider Love Unlimited collection that was built upon it, as an example of getting it right. “How can you stay true to a design that has been very successful, without just launching it in fresh colors?”.

Emerging designers are also having to balance viral popularity with long-term growth. Lubin points to Conner Ives, who recorded a 49% rise in demand from the second quarter of 2026 to the third quarter, according to the Lyst Index. “The Vintage Robe led desire, but demand was also spread across scarves, dresses and shirts,” she explains. Other success stories according to Lyst include Bottega Veneta and Chanel, both of which recorded strong demand in multiple categories. “Strength across categories spreads commercial risk and protects brand value. It also widens a brand’s reach, because each hero product brings in a different shopper, from a bag collector to sneaker enthusiasts.”.

Sources indicate that betting major on an already-popular product is a common path, whether it’s an oversized sneaker or a viral skirt. The brands that maintain that momentum and success, however, do so by looking forward. “Brands need to invest in the next reason to buy while the current hero funds the business,” indicates Alvarado. “The strategic advantage is building the next generation’s reason to purchase before the business loses the revenue supporting its current one.”.

How Celine’s Michael Rider Quietly Seized Fashion’s Attention

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that you can tell a lot about a designer by the scene backstage after a show.
  • Sources indicate that the co-ed summer 2027 runway was a blowout party hosted by Rider with models channeling twitchy upcoming-wave dancers, preppy ’80s croquet players, and the heroic DIY divas from Paris Is Burning.
  • In a recent development, in the garden of the National Archives Museum, friends of Rider like Hannah Einbinder, Tracee Ellis Ross, and Dan Levy milled around waiting for the designer to finish telling critics about his “intuitive” approach to fashion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you can tell a lot about a designer by the scene backstage after a show. Usually, it’s sweaty, manic, crammed with hangers-on—the fashion equivalent of an airport lounge during a blizzard. But on the unseasonably warm October day of Michael Rider’s most recent Paris runway show, the space was alive with Champagne toasts and bubbly conversation.

Sources indicate that the co-ed summer 2027 runway was a blowout party hosted by Rider with models channeling twitchy upcoming-wave dancers, preppy ’80s croquet players, and the heroic DIY divas from Paris Is Burning. Rider revealed new tailoring shapes for men, specifically loose, floppy blazers and slim cigarette-leg pants, cropped confidently above the ankle. A showstopping look of gleaming pink separates somehow avoided silliness. Rider’s signature styling took the edge off. A silver shimmering suit was mildly de-glammed by a jacket tied around the waist. A jaunty black hat topped off an outfit with a white long-sleeve shirt and shorts. Improbably, these wild ideas felt coherent—a hard-won sleight of hand.

In a recent development, in the garden of the National Archives Museum, friends of Rider like Hannah Einbinder, Tracee Ellis Ross, and Dan Levy milled around waiting for the designer to finish telling critics about his “intuitive” approach to fashion. Like something out of Lewis Carroll, a spread was unfurled on a long outdoor table. Waiters poured Champagne into a tower of coupes; editors licked homemade popsicles and bit into crunchy sandwiches of jambon-beurre. No one seemed like they had anywhere to be. This was the place to be.

In less than two years, Rider has cleaned the slate following Hedi Slimane’s shrunken, skinny rock era at Celine. He’s brought more accessible, artfully styled fashion to the stores. He’s delivered at least two hit shoes: the dirty white jazz lace-up, and, this past September, an immediately sold-out collaboration with Reebok that reissued the 1982 Freestyle Lo sneaker in decadent leather, in shades from oxblood to buttery yellow.

Sources indicate that in the process, his Celine has become a favorite among fashion-minded men. Ebon Moss-Bachrach, the tall Girls and The Bear actor, told me backstage that Rider’s menswear feels “masculine without any kind of footnote.” Youngjae, from the K-pop band TWS, explained the allure of Rider’s vision. “The Celine man is very free,” he said—just as the wild-haired designer burst outside for a smoke, laughing and relieved.

Wearing a standard-issue, backstage-friendly black crewneck sweater, Rider wasn’t exactly channeling the improvisational look of the brand he’s re-engineered in only a handful of highlights. He assumed the role of artistic director in 2025, succeeding Slimane. Before taking Celine’s reins, he put in time under Nicolas Ghesquière at Balenciaga (2004–08) and at Phoebe Philo–era Celine (2008–17). But the secret to the Rider Effect—his unique ability to conjure clarity from chaos—was a lesson he picked up during his tenure at Ralph Lauren.

According to recent reports, rider worked for the all-American designer as creative director of women’s Polo Ralph Lauren from 2018 until he decamped for Celine. Early on, he threw himself into staging his first “rig room.” A very Ralph tradition, the rig room is an installation of a fashion collection designed to be presented to Lauren internally—a fully immersive world complete with music, decor, props, and reference photos. Rider worked on his first one incessantly for two months. When Lauren arrived, he looked around in silence while Rider stood beside him, sweating in a navy blazer.

At last, Lauren asked, “Why do you want to confuse people?”.

In a recent development, “I think about that a lot,” confesses Rider when we speak in a circular antechamber at Celine’s Paris headquarters a few days after the show. Disappointing Lauren was a turning point for Rider. He had gotten the job designing Polo after 14 years in the upper echelons of European fashion. “Mixing references and confusing people was part of the game,” he remembers. “You elevated yourself and your brand through adjacencies and pastiche. Ralph was the total opposite.”.

Sources indicate that “I definitely appreciated going back to the States and hearing from a master: Be clear,” notes Rider. The ongoing tension of his current work lies in resolving his tendency toward anarchy with a desire for legibility. His Celine is layered and unfettered and fun. But it is also as clear, as the French say, as water on rocks.

Recent findings suggest that sitting in the same room where he and Philo “dumped our bags and met people” during his first stint at Celine, Rider looks calm and perfectly at home. Now that he’s at the helm of the 81-year-old LVMH maison founded by Céline and Richard Vipiana, the “rotonde” room has a few framed Latest Yorker cartoons propped on a wicker bench, some personalized thank-you cards to send, a pack of cigs, Evian, and not much else. Twinkly and alert, with no phone in sight, Rider wears a blue button-up, dark khaki pants, black canvas trainers, a gold Cartier watch, and some chunky rings. His hair sticks straight up like one of his inspirations: Isaac Mizrahi.

Industry observers note that mizrahi’s Unzipped documentary, which recently celebrated its 30th anniversary, was one of the references for the summer show. So, too, was another canonic ’90s documentary, Paris Is Burning, about the queer ballroom scene in late-’80s Manhattan. Both films look at the human side of fabulosity, something that interests Rider. Brands are the creations of curious, restless minds, and the best transcend desire, attracting something close to faith. Rider himself has been one of those believers, lusting after Ghesquière’s Balenciaga during his first real job, when he was just an underpaid teacher. (“I would have killed for something from there,” he says.) In his show notes, he wrote about “our desires and frustrations. Memories, moments that made us love fashion. Moments where you get a glimpse of possibility.”.

In practice, that looks like something you want to buy, but that has soul. Rider, like Lauren and Mizrahi, is a designer who makes clothing and accessories that feel just familiar enough to strike a nostalgic chord, but fresh enough that they can’t be replaced by trawling The RealReal. In his first Celine collection, shown in July 2025 under a sudden Parisian downpour, the looks bore a healthy pinch of Polo-honed prep: red blazers, diagonal-stripe ties, pressed jeans, loafers. Now that style is officially everywhere, with every middle-class menswear brand and fast-fashion factory churning out their own versions.

What separates Rider’s Celine is that it gets men excited to dress, claims Nordstrom men’s fashion director Jian DeLeon: “It triggers that lizard-brain impulse that inspires them to shop. They didn’t realize they wanted a bright-blue military jacket, and then when they see it in store, Rider’s design nuances—like oversized, ruched sleeves and slightly different blocks of color in the fabric—further satisfy the kinds of bells and whistles that men’s fashion enthusiasts nerd out about.”.

Industry observers note that in his first solo men’s presentation this past January, Rider brought his Ralph-perfected merchandising flair to Celine for a rig-room-esque installation of styling combinations that shouldn’t have worked—like a paisley tie layered beneath a red-string, hippie pendant necklace—and yet, did. Loafers in every shade played to an audience of ’90s kids who lusted after stacks of Benetton sweaters. Army jackets became accessories, belted around waists. It was American mall culture whipped through a blender with ready-to-wear refinement.

Industry observers note that rider’s Celine made an impact even earlier with his very first outing, the co-ed spring 2026 collection, shown in mid-2025. Soon after that range was available, Paul Anthony Kelly, who played nouveau John F. Kennedy Jr. in Ryan Murphy’s hit FX series Love Story, wore a Kennedy-ish Celine look: a white Oxford shirt, red-and-navy striped tie, navy blazer, jeans, white socks, loafers. The message was clear: Kelly had arrived—and so had Rider. Kelly’s stylist, Warren Alfie Baker, indicates he got hundreds of messages from people saying, “Oh my God, I need to go and buy that.” Why did he think it hit so hard? “What Michael does really well is it feels relatable,” Baker explained. “Everybody wanted to replicate it or have a version of it.”.

In a recent development, baker, who styles classic leading-men types like Glen Powell, Andrew Scott, and Andrew Garfield, says Rider’s work was heating up in Hollywood ahead of the fall awards season. “When you see a runway with 45 looks, and you’re like, ‘I could actually use 40 of them,’ that’s the dream scenario.”.

Slimane had introduced menswear to Celine in 2018 for the first time in the brand’s history with skinny black jeans, skinnier black ties, and shrunken leather jackets—an aesthetic driven more by rock-and-roll than red carpets. When he brought the brand to Los Angeles in late 2022 for an 87-look fashion show-cum-concert at the Wiltern, rockers including Iggy Pop, the Strokes, Interpol, and the Kills wore Slimane’s indie-sleaze uniforms to perform. “Celine’s past has been very skinny. Maybe some guys wouldn’t have known that they could wear it,” conceded Baker.

Sources indicate that rider’s Celine offers more elbow room, literally and otherwise. “It’s not such a rigid idea of how a man should dress,” says fashion commentator and stylist Nicky Bell, who has styled Mark Ronson in several Rider looks, including a custom leather jacket for this year’s Brit Awards. “Other menswear brands are too rigid: They want you to be this really formal, masculine man, or they want you to be super androgynous. He lands in this in-between space.”.

Recent findings suggest that born in 1980 to two do-gooder attorney parents in Washington DC, Rider was raised in an intellectual, progressive household well outside the fashion bubble. Musing on why he’s still drawn to things that are a little off, and the stalls at the flea market with “the mangiest, strangest assortment of clothing,” he states. “My parents are not materialistic in any way. There are nice things around, and they make things. My mom’s an incredible cook, there’s needlepoint, my dad [told] great stories. But it wasn’t a situation where aesthetic perfection was the goal.”.

“I was always in my own strange lane,” says Rider. “Everybody who seemed cool to me was on their own path.” His older cousin introduced him to the Grateful Dead, a lifelong love. Rider was, naturally, first drawn to the T-shirts—“the merch always brings me in”—but then became fascinated by the totality of Deadhead culture. “I was very attracted to the experimentation and freedom and fewer rules,” he says. “I like color, I like people who customize things, and I like weirdos.”.

Industry observers note that the Dead were a gateway into an adolescence full of experimentation. “I had all the phases,” Rider says, from Birkenstocks worn with Thorlo hiking socks, to hip-hop streetwear, to skate style that he finessed in shops like Green Barrel in Georgetown and Stüssy in the suburb of Potomac. He also dabbled in the all-American look he’d later help shape at Polo. “We went to public school and were proud of it, so preppy was a bad word, but everybody at my school worshipped Polo. They just wore it differently, and we mixed it all.”.

Rider’s still mixing. “It’s always been a lot of fun for me to get dressed,” he states. When he lived in Latest York City while at Ralph Lauren, he had standing movie nights at the Battery Park City cinema with the photographer Tommy Ton and designer Trevor Ballin (who works with him now at Celine), both friends. Ton, a street-style savant, loved seeing the outfits Rider would pull off at the cinema, like ankle-chopped Uggs with an Hermès shawl, or Grateful Dead bear–embroidered shorts. Levy says he could see Rider’s own vacation wardrobe in the women’s looks of the summer collection. “He demonstrates up to dinner in caftans and sandals, or harem pants.”.

Which can be hard to square with the fact that Rider went to Brown University with the intention of becoming a teacher. He moved to Oakland after graduating and taught ninth grade at a charter school. “Everyone was bigger than me,” indicates the petite designer. Living in the Bay Area, going out a lot, and experimenting with clothing, he eventually felt a pull to the creative world that he couldn’t shake, which would lead to him interning with his then hero, Ghesquière.

According to recent reports, rider, the former teacher, remains a perpetual student. He tells me, with a glance at his PR minder, that the kind of fashion profiles he loves—like Judith Thurman’s unvarnished 2005 Fresh Yorker story on Rei Kawakubo—aren’t really possible anymore. In the post-Galliano-meltdown, recession-hardened luxury landscape, publicly traded conglomerates protect their creative directors from criticism like the precious assets that they are.

Disconnecting is a skill he learned from Philo, his boss for nine years during a meteoric time at Celine. “She’s comfortable in privacy, and that allows her to be herself,” he notes. While he admires her discipline, he waxes nostalgic about how much fun they had together at the studio. “I laughed a lot, and enjoyed it a lot, and cared a lot,” he says. “And she made me want to work very, very, very hard.”.

So he painstakingly protects his distance—but doesn’t sacrifice his sense of humor in the process. You’ll see it in the pop of outrageous purple, a woolly outdoorsy fleece, those shimmering suits. There’s a sense that being too serious is just kind of sad. He likes when people talk about Celine as “good-time clothes” that they wear when they go out. “I would be mortified if anyone thought silliness was on the menu,” Rider says. Still, “Things are very funny to us, and that has to be felt somehow. I think humor is really stylish.”.

It has been revealed that eons have passed, seemingly, since Rider interned in the menswear department of Balenciaga in the mid-aughts. “Fashion for men was very fringe then,” he claims, remembering that the men’s collection at the label totaled maybe a dozen looks. At the time, Slimane’s strict silhouettes for Dior Homme were in; Rider wore some of that, along with the stiff selvedge APC jeans that became part of the ascent of #menswear. He recalls Ghesquière being obsessed at the time with making the ideal men’s wardrobe, from button-ups to parkas.

It has been revealed that “Menswear has completely opened up now,” Rider says. “It’s a different ball game. Because it’s so much broader now, and people have phones; people everywhere have access to so much and are engaged in more conversations. Not always for good, but it moves. The rules can move, and the goalposts can move.”.

Rider, after an almost Forrest Gump-y run of consistently being at the center of gravity—at Balenciaga, with Philo, and at Ralph Lauren—without having tried so hard to be there, is now the one doing the goalpost-moving. And he has no interest in hard rules or self-inflicted limitations.

“I think a lot of people who do this thing end up living, or trying to live out, the same story over and over,” he states.

In a recent development, he resists sheeplike notions of what’s considered cool—“this artist, this pottery, this lamp, this show space collaboration,” as he puts it. And he’s careful not to follow the flock too closely. “Paris is amazing, but Paris is insular,” claims Rider. “Everyone’s eating at the same canteen, gossiping about the same thing. There’s a gigantic world out there.”.

It has been revealed that so Rider keeps doing his own thing. He revels in American pop culture—he’s just as passionate about going to the multiplex near his weekend home in Normandy to see the latest Wicked as he is paging through those old World of Interiors magazines. He’s started weight-lifting, in the evenings. Learning Arabic is on his bucket list. And often he finds himself going back to his roots for inspiration.

In a recent development, every summer, he returns to Martha’s Vineyard, where his family has had a house since the 1970s. He loves its isolation, and its realness: “Against all odds, it has remained what it is. There’s no bridge, the airport’s still tiny, 85 percent of it is protected. There’s no Balenciaga.” On Martha’s Vineyard, he likes being out on the water.

“The most American thing about me is that I like to paddle,” he indicates, laughing. “I’m my best self in a canoe.” ✦.

A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 matter of GQ with the title “This Quiet American Has Fashion’s Attention.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Sticking needles in your face is a choice, but many who have done it, along with the experts administering them, will say the benefits of injectable fillers and muscle relaxants like Botox are worth the prick. Facial acupuncture takes a more holistic approach to smart aging—one that also claims to have wellness perks beyond simply aesthetics. Kim Ross, founder and CEO of Ora Method, explains the benefits, plus how and when to incorporate facial acupuncture into your routine.

In a recent development, acupuncture is a practice rooted in traditional Chinese medicine that uses ultrafine needles to stimulate circulation and support the body’s internal balance. Ross claims she first turned to the practice for her own digestive challenges and saw firsthand how effective it could be. That experience led her to start Ora Method, a NYC-based wellness practice specializing in acupuncture.

Facial acupuncture applies the same principles to the face. The treatment aims to gently boost circulation and support collagen production. “Many of our facials also include full-body acupuncture, because what shows up on the skin is often connected to what’s happening internally, like stress or hormonal fluctuations,” she explains. The treatment can also be layered with medical-grade red light therapy, along with guided meditation, which Ross notes works hand in hand with the acupuncture.

There are several. Ross notes that after a single acupuncture facial session, clients often notice less puffiness, smoother texture, and a subtle lift from the boost in circulation and lymphatic drainage. “Most people leave with slightly flushed, glowing skin,” she adds. The treatment can also help balance oil production, clear up mild breakouts, and improve skin texture.

It has been revealed that the bigger benefits build with consistency. “Acupuncture stimulates collagen production, which helps improve elasticity over time. It works with the skin and the muscles underneath instead of dramatically changing the face, so you end up with a healthier, more lifted version of your own features. That’s why so many of our clients see it as a long-term investment in their skin,” Ross adds.

Beyond the face, she also points out that how your skin looks has a lot to do with how your body feels on the inside. So, along with the face, there are perks to simultaneously doing full-body acupuncture.

Industry observers note that the treatment works across the whole face, but Ross states there are visible results for puffiness around the eyes and along the jawline, where fluid tends to build up. For TMJ sufferers, it also helps release tension in the jaw and facial muscles. The practice supports both lymphatic drainage and collagen production, so it’s a good fit for anyone who wants to refine their facial contours or improve tone and elasticity over time. “Many clients also notice their fine lines start to fade,” says Ross.

It has been revealed that you can actually do acupuncture even if you already have filler or have injected a muscle relaxant; Ross says it’s really about timing. “We ask clients to wait at least weeks after Botox or filler before booking a facial acupuncture treatment. That gives your injectables time to settle and keeps the treatment from interfering with your results,” she advises. It’s also crucial to note that each of these treatments yields different results. Acupuncture, filler, and neurotoxins like Botox each target different layers of the face and address signs of aging through completely different mechanisms. Botox temporarily blocks nerve signals to specific facial muscles, softening or freezing them so they don’t contract and leave indents in the skin, particularly where expression lines form on the forehead and around the eye area.

Sources indicate that acupuncture, on the other hand, uses hair-thin needles to create tiny microtraumas in the skin. Over time, the tiny punctures signal the body’s natural healing response and stimulate circulation, collagen, and elastin production. Dermal fillers work by filling in areas of the face that have hollowed out, lost volume, or need more sculpting with a substance like hyaluronic acid or poly-L-lactic acid.

Ross states that facial acupuncture is generally very gentle and requires little prep. Since the treatment uses ultrafine needles, most clients leave with slightly flushed, glowing skin. There’s typically no downtime, so you can go right back to your day. Skin tone and type are not factors; however, if you are sensitive, the pricks may cause more redness or irritation than in others.

Much like other professional treatments such as dermal fillers and Botox, Ross recommends pausing retinoids and any active exfoliants for five to seven days before an acupuncture facial, so your skin isn’t sensitive going into the treatment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

Industry observers note that if you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

In a recent development, remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

Drinking Tea Too Hot Could Be Bad For Your Health—Here's What To Know

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health.
  • Industry observers note that according to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease.
  • Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health. A recently published study followed nearly half a million adults in China for almost a decade, examining how tea-drinking habits related to their health. Researchers found that regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of vascular disease than non-tea drinkers. But one major caveat emerged: Those who reported drinking their tea “burning hot” had a higher risk of vascular disease.

Industry observers note that according to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease. But don't give up your daily tea habit quite yet. “This study is interesting, but we don't have a proven biological explanation yet,” Dr. Niraj Patel, medical director at Clara, indicates.

Dr. Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.

“It doesn’t look like this study has any proposed mechanism for why burning hot tea would increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” she explains. “However, we do know that drinks that are too hot can increase the risk of esophageal cancer by creating local injury and damage.”.

Industry observers note that that concern is supported by the World Health Organization's cancer research agency, which has classified drinking beverages hotter than 149°F as probably carcinogenic to humans. The classification specifically concerns esophageal cancer, though, so it doesn't explain the connection to vascular disease identified in the latest study.

The study didn’t identify a specific temperature at which drinking tea becomes detrimental to vascular health. And although researchers found an association between drinking extremely hot tea and vascular disease, that doesn't necessarily mean one causes the other.

ScienceDaily also notes that drinking tea at extremely high temperatures may diminish some of the health benefits associated with regular tea consumption.

Azarcon believes further research into tea's chemical makeup and how it may change at different temperatures could help answer some of the remaining questions.

"I'd say enjoy your tea, but don't feel like you need to drink it while it's scalding hot,” Patel suggests. “There's a difference between brewing tea with hot water and actually drinking it at that temperature. Letting it cool for a few minutes is an easy precaution and doesn't require giving up something you enjoy.".

So while I don’t plan on giving up my tea habit any time soon, I am definitely making extra sure that I let my cup sit out a little longer before taking that first sip.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I will keep rolling down until my best shirt rolls off,” warbles Cameron Winter on “The Rolling Stone,” the opening track of his 2024 solo debut Heavy Metal. That album later became the basis of the Geese frontman’s historic December 2025 performance at Carnegie Hall, which was filmed and subsequently turned into a captivating concert film by Oscar-winning director Paul Thomas Anderson. A year later, Winter—and perhaps you—will now have a new best shirt to roll off.

PTA’s Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall, which was shot on 35mm and 16mm film, will hit select theaters nationwide on Friday. As a reward to the Geeseheads and steadfast cinephiles who attend the 35mm screenings, distributor Janus Films produced a limited-edition run of merch (many such cases!) that can only be purchased IRL at select participating theaters. Which is to say, acquiring this merch…takes miles.

But if you’re looking at the Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall T-shirts ($40) and baseball hats ($35) and thinking, “Wow, those look a lot like the maximalist, erudite wares from Boot Boyz Biz,” that’s because they were in fact designed by two of the Chicago brand’s current outposts, Now-Time and Mike’s Deli.

In an email, the Now-Time/Mike’s Deli team mentioned that they drew inspiration from Carnegie Hall’s history and architecture. “We looked to the building itself as a visual archive to draw from, seeking forms that resonated with the performance across time,” they wrote. “Familiar architectural details took on a new heightened significance, knowing what was happening inside. In Carnegie Hall’s classic horseshoe layout we saw the camera’s panoramic intent. Outside on the 19th-century facade we found typographic elements that paralleled the energy of the event.” A very Winteresque explanation, in a way. Ideal for any enigmatic T-shirt enthusiast.

If you, too, would like to participate in the seeking forms and panoramic intent of Winter’s moving piano stylings on one winter’s night in Manhattan, you better start a-walking to the nearest 35mm-equipped cinema near you.

GQ staffers Jordan Bowman and Gerald Ortiz testing out the merchandise.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

I am what you might call a problem sleeper. I often toss and turn for hours before falling asleep. Sleep aids don’t work on me (if I’m sick and take NyQuil, I end up with insomnia rather than a deep slumber). I’ll wake up at witching hour and worry about something before falling back asleep. All of this has been known to wreak havoc on my face. After nights when I barely clock five hours, I wake up to dark circles, a duller complexion, and puffy skin. But Augustinus Bader’s The Overnight Restorative Cream works like an insurance policy for sleepless nights.

Skin repairs itself overnight, and just like every other function in your body, it doesn’t do it as well when you don’t sleep. This can lead to inflammation, a damaged barrier, and even accelerated aging (not exactly what I want to hear as a chronic insomniac). While many beauty products have promised to fake the appearance of eight hours of sleep, Augustinus Bader’s upcoming cream has a unique rosehip extract that mimics the effects of melatonin. While the hormone regulates your sleep cycle, melatonin could also be good for your skin. One study even found that it might have antiaging properties thanks to its ability to protect cells. This cream is also made with both polyglutamic and hyaluronic acid to seal in hydration. There’s cica to calm skin and combat inflammation. And of course, since it’s an Augustinus Bader product, there’s also an advanced form of TFC8, the brand’s proprietary ingredient, which facilitates communication between skin cells for repair and renewal.

In a recent development, since using this moisturizer, my skin looks clear, toned, and glowy most mornings. While I do look bright-eyed and bushy-tailed when I manage to sleep that long and use this cream, my skin looks just as good when I get six hours of sleep. Or—gulp—five. (Any less and my brain isn’t even functioning enough to examine the state of my skin.) My next trick will be to find a face cream that puts me to sleep, but since products can’t, at the current moment, work miracles (including this one), I’ll settle for one that helps mitigate the effects of a bad night.

#42926. How Luxury Brands Should Show Up for UAE’s National Day

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1558 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

How Luxury Brands Should Show Up for UAE’s National Day

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, december in the United Arab Emirates begins with one of the country’s most significant celebrations: UAE National Day, officially known as Eid Al Etihad.
  • Recent findings suggest that as the luxury industry invests more in the Middle East, holiday shopping moments around Eid and Ramadan have ranked high on brands’ priority lists.
  • For those who live and work in the UAE, the occasion carries a significance that extends well beyond a public holiday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, december in the United Arab Emirates begins with one of the country’s most significant celebrations: UAE National Day, officially known as Eid Al Etihad. On December 2, 1971, six emirates (Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah) formally united to establish the United Arab Emirates, under the vision of the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan. Ras Al Khaimah joined the federation on February 10, 1972, completing the union of seven emirates.

Recent findings suggest that as the luxury industry invests more in the Middle East, holiday shopping moments around Eid and Ramadan have ranked high on brands’ priority lists. To expand their reach, brands should look beyond these two tentpoles, starting with National Day, which this year marks the 55th anniversary of the UAE’s formation on December 2-3.

For those who live and work in the UAE, the occasion carries a significance that extends well beyond a public holiday. “What makes the UAE particularly special is that its national identity is strong enough to embrace people from all over the world without losing its own character,” notes Ahmad Al Gergawi, an Emirati and founder of UAE-based creative agency Dyemension A, which has worked with brands ranging from Cartier and Vacheron Constantin to Birkenstock. “It is a country where Emirati heritage and global perspectives coexist, and where people from different backgrounds are able to contribute to its story.”.

In 2025, Birkenstock collaborated with Dyemension A for their National Day celebrations, employing Emirati talent across their production.

This year’s celebrations come after a particularly challenging period for the region, shaped in part by the US-Israeli war on Iran and its wider economic repercussions. For the retail industry, the impact has been felt through increased costs of transporting goods and a slowdown in tourism.

According to recent reports, against this backdrop, the importance of the local consumer has come into sharper focus, particularly as UAE residents have continued to support the market and luxury brands. Firras Alwahabi, founder and managing director of Faux Consultancy, a Dubai-based public relations manufacturer whose clients include Loewe, Guerlain and Zegna, says, “I think this year’s National Day will carry particular significance. The UAE has experienced a challenging year, and I think there will be an even stronger sense of appreciation, pride and solidarity among those who call the country home.” But how should brands show up?

Industry observers note that for luxury brands, this presents an opportunity to consider how they participate in the country’s national celebrations. But, as Alwahabi points out, National Day is not necessarily an easy occasion for fashion brands to interpret. National Day is different from Ramadan and Eid, Alwahabi says, where occasion dressing is more clearly defined around the religious holidays. It is not an occasion where people typically dress a particular way, which makes it more challenging for fashion brands to translate into a capsule collection or a specific product offering. “National Day is less about shopping for the occasion and more about the experience and connection people are looking for. Customers want to celebrate, express their pride and share meaningful moments with their families and communities,” says Reda Keddaji, general manager of Tryano, the luxury department store at Yas Mall in Abu Dhabi.

Alwahabi’s advice is for brands to rethink their approach. “Rather than creating another product or collection for every occasion, I think the opportunity lies in finding more meaningful and relevant ways to participate,” he says.

Samara Punjabi, CEO of Timeless Group, which owns Palm Angels, Temperley London and Kat Maconie and distributes labels including Off-White, Judith Leiber and Dunhill, believes localization needs to go beyond adapting a global campaign with local colors or messaging. “The UAE is a significant market for international luxury brands, but understanding its cultural identity goes far beyond commercial opportunities. National Day is deeply personal, and brands need to recognize the emotional connection people have with the country,” she indicates.

In celebration of UAE National Day, customers will be able to personalise their Off-White pieces with UAE-inspired motifs through an exclusive heat-press patch bar.

According to recent reports, for Timeless Group, National Day is an opportunity to spotlight existing offerings rather than launch new products. Palm Angels’ Dubai-exclusive capsule and Judith Leiber’s Dubai number plate clutch and bag inspired by the Dubai chocolate and pistachio croissant are available all year, but are being presented as National Day edits. For this year's celebrations, Off-White is developing exclusive artwork featuring Dubai landmarks and cultural references such as karak tea and the falcon. Customers will also be able to personalize T-shirts through an in-store heat-press experience. “The biggest opportunity for international brands is to move from simply marketing to the region to actively creating with the region. That is where meaningful cultural connections and long-term brand loyalty are built,” claims Punjabi.

Palm Angels collaborated with Dubai-based creative community SNS to curate looks featuring pieces from the brand.

According to recent reports, for Al Gergawi, the distinction between referencing a culture and genuinely involving its community is key. He points to Birkenstock’s National Day collaboration with his agency last year, which involved Emirati talent across the production, from actors and the director to the set designer and crew. “It’s not about placing an Emirati face in an advertisement or incorporating cultural references for the sake of relevance. It’s about genuinely investing in the people, creativity and communities that make this region what it is,” he says. “Birkenstock isn’t simply speaking to the UAE community. It’s creating with them.”.

According to recent reports, at Tryano, the emphasis is on experience rather than product. Its National Day activation will run from November 27 to December 6, with the main in-store experience on December 1. The program will bring Emirati hospitality into the store through a Talli demonstration by an Emirati artisan, an Emirati-inspired Majlis setting and henna painting. Homegrown brands, Keddaji notes, often have a closer connection to local heritage, craftsmanship and identity. International brands can also participate, provided their contribution feels relevant, respectful and authentic.

Not every initiative needs to be a public-facing campaign. Etoile Group, which operates boutiques across seven countries in the region, including brands such as Chanel, Etro, Ralph Lauren, Valentino, Tod’s and Aquazzura, says it will send National Day gifts to its UAE national VIP clients across its brands and celebrate employees.

Industry observers note that while National Day remains an underexplored moment on the UAE cultural calendar for international brands, Al Gergawi believes cultural engagement cannot be confined to a handful of occasions. “UAE consumers are increasingly discerning. They can tell the difference between a brand that engages with the culture organically and one that appears only for a seasonal campaign. Culture is rooted in values, and those values should not be confined to activations around Emirati Women’s Day, National Day or Ramadan. Brands need a year-round strategy that carries cultural understanding through their communications, identity and commitment to community empowerment,” he claims.

In a recent development, miral Youssef, president of Kering Middle East, Africa and India, says this approach is reflected in the group’s work in the UAE. “Our relationship with the UAE and its communities goes well beyond National Day. It is built throughout the year, through meaningful collaborations, shared experiences and the people we work with. UAE National Day is an opportunity to celebrate these relationships, rather than create them for the occasion,” she says.

Bottega Veneta spotlighted Emirati weaving traditions in parallel with the house intrecciato weave.

Industry observers note that she points to collaborations across Kering’s Houses with regional creative talent. This year, Boucheron hosted “Hug My Land” with Emirati photographer Hussain AlMossawi and homegrown café Inner Child. Pomellato’s “The Art of Iconic Craftsmanship” brought its Iconica collection together with five women designers from the region, including Emirati studio One Third Studio. In October, Bottega Veneta’s “When Your Own Initials Are Enough” at Keturah Cactus Park in Dubai brought Emirati weaving traditions into dialogue with the house’s Italian intrecciato technique through its collaboration with Irthi, a Sharjah-based organization dedicated to preserving and reinterpreting the UAE’s traditional crafts. Other Kering brands are marking National Day with dedicated activations: Bottega Veneta will welcome guests to its boutiques at Mall of the Emirates, The Dubai Mall and Abu Dhabi for artistic experiences led by Emirati artists, while Saint Laurent will draw on the UAE’s tradition of hospitality through intimate in-store activations.

Earlier this year Boucheron collaborated with Hussain AlMossawi, presenting his photography of UAE’s architectural heritage as collectible postcards.

Youssef’s advice to brands is to collaborate rather than decorate, giving local creatives, artisans and designers a genuine role; invest in local talent beyond a single celebration; and be present throughout the year. “Meaningful relationships are built through consistency, mutual respect and a long-term commitment to the community,” she states.

Industry observers note that as brands begin planning their calendars for 2027, National Day should sit alongside other key moments in the UAE’s cultural calendar, including Emirati Women’s Day and Ramadan, as well as events such as Art Dubai. The opportunity is to build a calendar that reflects a deeper understanding of the UAE, its people and its cultural landscape, rather than approaching each occasion as a one-off marketing opportunity. As Al Gergawi adds: “When the cultural connection is genuine, the commercial value will often follow naturally.”.

When Converse and Noah collaborated for the first time earlier this year, the most surprising thing was that it’d taken so long for them to link up. The sneaker OGs and Upcoming York menswear mavens make as much sense together as peanut butter and jelly—both brands flow effortlessly between worlds, embraced by punks and preps and hoopers and skaters alike. Thankfully, the duo have been making up for lost time, kicking their partnership off with a couple of killer Chuck 70s in the spring before putting out an understated banger of a spin on the Louie Lopez 2 over the summer. Now, they’re capping off their banner year with one last go-round—another jazzed-up Chuck Taylor that’s about as holiday-ready as it gets.

It has been revealed that just in time for turkey season, Noah has wrapped the Converse Chuck 70 Low in one of the most beloved patterns in menswear: Black Watch tartan. The green, navy, and black plaid was originally worn by squadrons patrolling the Scottish Highlands in the 18th century, with its subdued tones meant to help wearers blend into their surroundings. Over the past several decades, it’s been embraced by fashion at large, but particularly Trad Ivy enthusiasts, who tend to sport the striking tartan on everything from sport coats and scarves during the colder months.

In addition to the sharp Black Watch canvas uppers, Noah made a handful of other subtle changes to the classic silhouette, adding its branding to the “license plate” on the shoe’s heel, removing the wing tongue stitch, and swapping in a woven tongue tag. The kicks feature the standard white laces but also come with a mustard yellow pair for an extra boost of color.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking to dress festively but aren’t all that into freaky patterned sweaters, the latest Converse x Noah Chuck 70 Low might just be the ticket. The shoes drop tomorrow, November 19, for $112 via both Converse and Noah.

Kering Hires Group Pricing Director: Why It Matters

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kering has appointed Francisco Ochando to the newly created role of group pricing director, the organization confirmed on Wednesday.
  • According to his LinkedIn profile, Ochando previously worked at Inditex, Calvin Klein and Nike, most recently as director of planning in charge of lifestyle footwear at the sporting giant, based in the Netherlands.
  • Pricing architecture is typically the remit of merchandising teams at the brand level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kering has appointed Francisco Ochando to the newly created role of group pricing director, the organization confirmed on Wednesday. Ochando, who took up the position on November 16, reports to Marilyne Trebus, Kering’s chief product officer, who in turn reports to Carlo Mocci, the group’s chief client officer.

According to his LinkedIn profile, Ochando previously worked at Inditex, Calvin Klein and Nike, most recently as director of planning in charge of lifestyle footwear at the sporting giant, based in the Netherlands. In his fresh role at Kering, and according to his LinkedIn, he will be “leading the group-wide pricing strategy across all Kering houses and geographies, driving sustainable revenue growth, brand value creation and pricing excellence”.

Pricing architecture is typically the remit of merchandising teams at the brand level. What, then, is the rationale for having someone oversee it at group level?

Recent findings suggest that as part of the “ReconKering” strategy unveiled at the group’s Capital Markets Day in April, CEO Luca de Meo stated he would build a “streamlined group platform”, organized around five “hubs”, including a client hub led by Mocci. “It is not a question of centralization. It’s a rebalance,” de Meo said.

This strategy makes sense in the short term due to the need for greater discipline and alignment after years of underperformance, according to Goldman Sachs analyst Erwan Rambourg. “This nomination [of Ochando ] comes across as quite consistent with what the group is trying to achieve,” he says.

During an interview with Vogue Business in October 2025, de Meo also outlined his ambition to take a more strategic approach to managing the group’s brand portfolio. “We need to ensure there’s no cannibalization between the brands, and strategically target different types of clients with each brand based on what we’ve achieved so far,” he noted.

The French luxury group’s new CEO attended fashion week in Milan and Paris. He shares his first take with Vogue Business.

Industry observers note that at Capital Markets Day, he explained this further by saying that Balenciaga is best positioned to capture the Gen Z audience as “one of the brands that better understands the vibes of the new generation”, while Bottega Veneta should have a different positioning with a higher-end clientele. And pricing is a significant component of this strategic approach.

Ochando’s appointment comes at a time when the industry is grappling with pricing challenges, amid criticism of so-called “greedflation” — the idea that many luxury brands raised prices too aggressively, and too quickly, during the post-Covid luxury boom.

“Pricing has been an glitch for the industry in the last three years, as aspirational consumers have been priced out,” Mario Ortelli, managing partner of Ortelli & Co, says. “There’s a disconnect between the perceived value and the cost of the product. Appointing a pricing director is an organizational attempt to address the situation. This newly introduced role can help in fine-tuning the pricing architecture across brands, and centralize competitive intelligence on the pricing of competitors.”.

Sources indicate that as Kering’s largest brand Gucci navigates a turnaround, it has taken selective price cuts, according to Bernstein analyst Luca Solca. For example, he notes that global prices for Spring/Summer 2026’s Mercato tote bag were reduced by 20% to 25% (from €2.600 to €1.950 for the small version, in leather, in France). “Our data indicates that Gucci continues to work on increasing brand accessibility,” Solca wrote in a note in July. For example, Gucci launched at its resort 2026 show the Giglio, a tote bag whose large canvas edition is priced at €1,800.

Ochando will need to support brands in their efforts to win back middle-income consumers, either by introducing newly introduced product lines at more accessible price points or by selectively lowering prices. Both approaches will need to be carefully done to ensure affordability while preserving the brand equity.

“Gucci has lowered prices, notably on products from previous designers that will be discontinued, and the sector overall has come out with more palatable price points throughout,” Rambourg says, noting that the work to appeal to more price-sensitive customers is not Gucci-specific. “It holds true for Chanel, Dior, Burberry and many others, hopefully gradually reversing the negative impacts of post-Covid greedflation on end demand.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he mentioned he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard.

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Industry observers note that transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

In a recent development, place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very promptly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a latest personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

It has been revealed that scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

Inside Gap’s ‘Fashiontainment’ Era

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • in January as the organization’s first chief entertainment officer, bringing two decades of experience from Nickelodeon, Viacom and Paramount Global, where she led collaborations with brands from Nike to Stella McCartney.
  • With CEO Richard Dickson — another fashion import who joined from Mattel in 2023 — Kaufman is leading entertainment strategy across Gap, Banana Republic, Old Navy and Athleta.
  • At the Vogue Business Global Summit: Upcoming York, Dickson and Kaufman took part in their first joint interview to discuss the importance of relevance in today’s retail environment, and how to pull off an entertainment playbook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pam Kaufman joined Gap Inc. in January as the organization’s first chief entertainment officer, bringing two decades of experience from Nickelodeon, Viacom and Paramount Global, where she led collaborations with brands from Nike to Stella McCartney. Now, she’s moved in-house with a retailer that’s ready to reclaim brand storytelling and relevance for a fresh generation.

With CEO Richard Dickson — another fashion import who joined from Mattel in 2023 — Kaufman is leading entertainment strategy across Gap, Banana Republic, Old Navy and Athleta. It’s a new approach to marketing that speaks to the immersion of fashion in culture, across sports, music, gaming and Hollywood. It’s also an approach only made possible by the work Dickson has done in his first three years to clean up Gap’s inventory and discounting cycle. With the fundamentals in place, Gap can have more fun, starting with a partnership with American boy band JYT, a group of teens new to the scene and embarking on a mall tour and capsule collection with Gap.

At the Vogue Business Global Summit: Upcoming York, Dickson and Kaufman took part in their first joint interview to discuss the importance of relevance in today’s retail environment, and how to pull off an entertainment playbook. The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vogue: You just had your first substantial campaign rollout since you joined, Pam. I was excited to see that it was a mall tour, as someone who grew up in the ‘90s. How did you land on this concept, and what does the full campaign look like that you brought to life?

Pam Kaufman: First of all, it’s great to be here. Thank you for having us. The mall tour is going extremely well. It’s a great time to be in this space, because the generation ‘now’ — Generation Z, Generation Alpha — is really seeking live experiences. They’re going to the movies, they’re going to the malls.

It has been revealed that the band we’re working with is JYT, and this is a partnership that Gap created with Wexler Records and Republic Records to work with latest artists and take them on a journey through a docuseries, a mall tour, a camp tour, a capsule collection. And so, the mall was a very massive part of the opportunity to work with them because, as you know, Gap started as a mall brand, one of the most vital fashion mall brands in the world, and so that was the perfect jumping-off point for us. Early responses have been phenomenal. We’ve seen a lot of people really get excited about bringing back the iconic American boy band. And the plan is not to just put Gap products in a docuseries; the plan is to truly understand the story of these boys. The capsule collection is designed by each member of the band. So we are not in it for the short term. This is a long-term partnership with them.

Industry observers note that vogue: Richard, you have experience blending brand and entertainment from your Mattel days. How have you taken that experience to Gap, and have you seen more brands embrace this approach to entertainment?

Richard Dickson: To me, every brand is a story. And you need to be able to tell your stories where consumers are to be relevant, with relevant content and narratives that tell the brand story. So in that dynamic, experiences become a really important part of the narrative. And so for Gap, when you go back to the origin story of the brand — what was the brand’s DNA? It’s not random that we’re working with the music industry — the context of the content for Gap is around the celebration of music, originality, identity and individuality. And so, Pam’s work is exactly that. It’s synonymous with the brand’s DNA and its rightful place. It’s authentic, because music and originality are authentic to Gap.

Vogue: I want to hear about how you met and what those early conversations were like, and the vision that you saw for this role.

RD: Pam and I started decades ago as colleagues and friends working at different companies.

PK: He was trying to turn a doll into a brand; I was trying to turn a sponge into a brand, because I was at Nickelodeon at the time.

RD: She had a sponge, I had a doll, and basically, we were collaborating —.

Industry observers note that RD: It was about that combination of understanding what a brand could be beyond the product itself, and then the methodology of how to do that — that’s not easy. You need to be fluent in that space, and sometimes when you come into a brand of our size, we’re very category-centric. You become a machine. And to some extent, you get so significant that you get too complex to be able to pivot and be agile and see beyond the machine. So you need leaders who can come in and challenge the status quo, and introduce fresh ideas and questions, and surround the beauty of the legacy with different thinking, different talent, and different ways of approaching how to stay relevant. We’re lucky to have Pam, and to have created this position that takes our iconic brands and personifies them in ways that create relevance and drive revenue.

Troye Sivan in Gap’s ‘Let Loose’ campaign.

Vogue: Can a clothing brand have fans in the same way that Barbie or SpongeBob does?

PK: There are a lot of Gap fans out there. These are really established iconic American brands — Gap, Banana Republic, Old Navy and Athleta. So the job is to understand what each brand stands for, and then figure out how to amplify the brands through culture, which, quite frankly, it’s not that different from what we’ve done with Barbie or SpongeBob. It’s figuring out what makes them matter, and then amplifying them. And in this entertainment role, that’s through licensing — so partnering with the entertainment companies, sports leagues, gaming companies. That’s where culture is created. It’s not a one-size-fits-all approach. And then there’s content. How do you create stories that feel like they could only come from a certain brand?

In a recent development, vogue: What about loyalty? Do you think fashion fans are less loyal?

Industry observers note that RD: Yeah, I do. And as a brand, you have to recognize that it’s now a dialogue with your consumer, not a monologue. I mean, there was a chapter where brands were like, ‘This is the way. This is what we are. This is who we are. Like it, don’t like it, learn to love it.’ That doesn’t work today. So fueling brand fandom is actually about having that dialogue and giving them more of what they love, surprising them, delighting them, feeding that fuel that ultimately creates more fandom. That is the flywheel of any narrative that becomes relevant. The key to doing that is by keeping up with momentum and moving at the speed of culture. And that’s not easy. But ultimately I think out of all the industries, I find fashion to be a much more fan-driven business.

Industry observers note that PK: I just want to build off what Richard mentioned. We have stores. That’s an opportunity for us to turn our store into a stage, an experience. In entertainment IP, we were on the other side, trying to take our IP and put it into retail. So it’s fun now to be here, having my own stage, obviously working very closely with the brand team, and saying, ‘Look what’s coming out of Hollywood. This is such an exciting moment. How can we amplify some of these incredible films, or sporting events, and create a fun experience for our customer?’ So, that’s another way to reach fans through our own retail stores.

Vogue: Richard, you mentioned the tech giant having to move at the speed of culture. How do you set up a company that has the ability to move that promptly, even if it feels risky?

Recent findings suggest that RD: It certainly is risky, but, again, if you don’t take swings, you’re never going to hit. So you’ve got to be agile and ultimately encourage the organization, at the highest level, to take chances. It’s not random; we have a playbook. We know what’s on-brand, and you encourage the organization to extend that strategy in relevant ways. And if we’re trying to get more relevant, and you have a brand framework that people understand, and then you encourage creativity within that, you’d be amazed at people’s ideas. Then you can say, ‘Yes, let’s go try that.’ That is a culture. Strategies can be copied. We talk about our playbook all day long. It’s not the secret sauce. What really makes it is culture, and culture is human.

According to recent reports, and we’re a large business. It’s complex. It’s billions of dollars and millions of units, and you’ve got to get the right size at the right place at the right time, with the right fabric, with the right fit, with the right… it’s torture. It’s a tough business. So to be able to transparently work together as a team, share what’s not working more than what is working, you’d be surprised at how many things you could tackle when you work with people who see what you see, can acknowledge what’s wrong, and work together to get it right.

Vogue Business’s executive editor, Hilary Milnes, alongside Pam Kaufman, chief entertainment officer, and Richard Dickson, CEO.

Vogue: We spoke in the past about the work you did to clean up Gap’s inventory, getting out of the discounting cycle. How do you see that side of the job compared to an entertainment strategy? You have to have the right foundation in place before you can think about these things.

In a recent development, RD: We weren’t ready for Pam. We went through about a three-year cycle of what we call fixing fundamentals. It’s complicated, and we had a lot of work to do to reorganize the company. We had become more about the stuff than the story.

PK: And the red windows, the signs.

It has been revealed that RD: The signs, the sales, the 50% off. We lost our narrative around product, and that’s what we’ve been working so hard to get back. And in the context of that, it’s been a true ‘perform while you transform’, because we are public, so we have a lot of responsibility. We laid the groundwork for all of that, so we could build momentum and bring in true storytellers and begin the next phase. That’s an exciting latest frontier that we’re privileged to be part of with a manufacturer that has so much legacy. You feel a responsibility to get it to where it needs to be, and then pass it to the next generation to ultimately make it even better.

Vogue: What advice would you give any brand leaders who want to step into this world with their own strategy around celebrities, culture and entertainment?

PK: I would say to any brand, are you ready? Do you have the right product? Do you have the right leadership team? And then most importantly, it’s really fun to meet with everybody in the industry that wants to work with us, but out of the 50, 70 meetings we’re taking with talent or studios or leagues, finding the one or the few that work for us is really hard. It’s a little bit of art and science. It’s not quantity, it is quality, and that’s what Richard has emphasized. We don’t want a million partners. We want the ones that really make the most sense.

Vogue: We have an audience question: ‘What earns consumer attention in the US right now? Is it editorial, celebrity, retail partnerships, collaborations, or something else?’.

According to recent reports, RD: I would wrap all of that up into, yes. And relevance. Relevance is an unlock for a variety of different outcomes. It’s sort of the invitation to the attention. Once you have that attention, what are you doing with it? There are a lot of brands that have relevance, but then what are you selling? How did you make money? But first, you have to capture attention. That sounds easy, but it is so hard. And so, you need to find your brand voice, and then that becomes the distinction. ‘OK, how do I get that story across and become relevant to a consumer to get that attention?’ But if that attention doesn’t convert to revenue, you’re sort of only halfway there. At the end of the day, it’s the product that creates enduring relationships.
