For Pura d'Or, it's this organic beard oil. It's the best value on this list, at $3 per fluid ounce. Given how rapidly you can go through beard oil—just think, if you're applying up to twice a day, that dollar-per-ounce math becomes vital. So, in addition to being my budget pick, this also gets my recommendation as the best beard oil for big beards.

Of course, it's only important if the formula measures up—and here, it does. There are two carrier oils, argan and jojoba, along with a bit of grapefruit peel and some sandalwood essential oil for both a natural scent and a touch of antimicrobial powers. It's a great beard oil for anyone, no matter how major your bank account, but if you're bearding on a budget, you'll appreciate how much goodness Pura d'Or packs into a few bucks.

Sources indicate that blind Barber's tonka-tinged oil is wonderful for the guy who wants to moisturize skin and whiskers with the same product. It wears extremely light—so much so that my oily skin barely registers its presence—and I find its carrier-oil-centric and shea-butter-forward formula especially comforting on the skin. It should be noted that this formula includes artificial perfume, so fragrance-averse individuals should steer clear. But for those of us who want a special scent, a flake-free beard, and soothed skin, Blind Barber's beard oil does it all.

It has been revealed that while I'd use most of the above options as both a hair oil and a beard oil, Aesop's is one where I think of it as a hair oil first and foremost. It brings control without making things look greasy, while trapping moisture and stopping frizz. I'll use it in short hair to tame down the sides, in medium lengths (mixed with a cream or clay) for added shine, or in long hair to prevent split ends. Then, once my hair's settled up, I'll run my hands through my beard afterward. So, if you want a great hair oil with beard benefits, Aesop's is the winner.

Since the beginning of the men's grooming boom, I've been waiting for the big designer fashion houses to start catering to guys with facial hair. For now, Tom Ford's beard oil stands alone. So, how does the designer oil stack up against our everyday favorites? After trying it out, I can tell you it’s better as a fragrance than a beard oil, but the scent alone earns it a spot in this guide.

It has been revealed that the tobacco vanilla fragrance is much more sophisticated than what we’re used to seeing, or smelling, in this space. The scent puts an emphasis on vanilla, and you just need one or two pumps for full coverage. Considering the price and the name on the bottle, we were shocked to find this oil comes in a plastic pump bottle, but that fragrance. If you want to buy beard oil as a gift, this premium conditioning oil is a step up over your average Amazon brand, even if it doesn't soften coarse hair as well as some of our other options.

It has been revealed that if you have sensitive skin—or if you're afraid of your beard oil clashing with your daily cologne—then Marlowe makes one of the only fragrance-free beard oils. Most beard oil formulas contain both essential oils and some type of perfume oil (or, parfum, for my fellow ingredients detectives), which can be risky for your skin, follicles, and pores, so it’s nice to have an option for acne-prone and sensitive skin types.

This beard oil couldn’t be simpler—and I mean that in a good way. Marlowe No. 143 has an all-oil formula and just four ingredients: safflower seed oil, sunflower seed oil, corn oil, and soybean oil. That’s it. Considering the average beauty product contains up to a dozen ingredients we can’t even pronounce, it’s a refreshing change. Although, I have to say, if you want the softest possible beard, Honest Amish also makes a fragrance-free oil.

Most guys use beard oil to tame flyaways. But what if you want the thickest, fullest beard possible? In that case, I’d recommend reaching for Bevel’s oil. This brand makes skin and hair products for Black men, but anyone with coarse or curly hair can benefit from their products. GQ contributor Timothy Beck Werth reports that this oil gave him a thicker-looking beard without excess frizz, which isn't easy to do. (BTW, that’s as much as you can expect from any beard oil, so please don’t fall for the “beard growth serums” you’ll find all over the internet.).

Sources indicate that for parched facial hair, the grapeseed, macadamia, jojoba, and argan oil will condition your beard and add a healthy shine. For beneath the scruff, the avocado and primrose oil with soothe your skin without clogging up your pores and follicles. Werth notes this beard oil instantly softened his facial hair, and he also liked the sweeter smell of the macadamia-based formula. Most beard oils opt for woodsy fragrances, and the more subtle scent profile here is a nice surprise, he explains.

According to recent reports, anthony’s conditioning beard oil is a 2-in-1 product—a pre-shave oil and regular beard oil. That approach can be risky, since a lot of multipurpose products try to be everything and succeed at nothing, but luckily that’s not the case here. If you regularly cycle between clean-shaven, stubble, and full-on lighthouse keeper, then you can still use this product daily. As a pre-shave oil, it moisturizes the skin and softens facial hair for a smoother shave with fewer morning-after red bumps. As a beard oil, it hydrates, then locks in that moisture so your beard stays soft and shiny all day. I found the consistency to be somewhere in between a leave-in conditioner gel and a traditional oil, making it thicker and less messy to apply.

The oil also has an herbaceous, minty fragrance that’s so refreshing it feels like aromatherapy every time you run it through your hair. That’s because the formula is full of ingredients that smell good, feel good, and actually help your skin and hair. It uses carrier oils like soybean and castor to deliver skin-pleasing and antimicrobial botanicals such as rosemary, basil, tea tree oil, eucalyptus, and spearmint. And on the hydration front, calendula and olive oil nourish your whiskers into their softest, fluffiest selves. Because of the more complex fragrance and ingredients profile, this wouldn’t be my pick for guys with sensitive skin. Still, it’s a multi-functional serum you’ll look forward to using every day.

Sources indicate that lots of beard oils promise to get flyaways under control, yet those rogue hairs keep popping up. So, what do you do? Instead of trying yet another oil, try reaching for a product that’s more of a leave-in conditioner for your beard. We’ve previously praised Zeus’s beard brushes, but the California-based brand also makes a beard serum that deserves a spot in your bathroom cabinet. I love that this beard oil has the simplest possible ingredients list: sweet almond oil, soybean oil, argan seed oil, trihydroxystearin, avocado oil, and fragrance.

Industry observers note that the only multi-syllable ingredient there is a simple thickening agent, which gives this refined beard oil a gel-like consistency. That thicker formula will also put flyaways in their place. The very subtle fragrance is more Mediterranean than winter pine forest (we tested the Verbena Lime version), but you can also opt for a fragrance-free formula if you have sensitive skin or allergies. The plastic bottle uses an air pump, letting you get every last drop of oil. For clean freaks who hate the messiness and spillage that always comes with beard oil application, this is another bonus.

Tired of being left out of couple’s skincare night just because those stupid sheet masks won’t hold onto your glorious beard? Cardon’s got you, boo. Actually, this bead oil hack is perfect for guys who only sparingly use beard oil on an as-needed basis.

The bamboo and charcoal sheet mask is specially shaped for guys with beards, and each mask comes with a dose of beard oil made with argan and jojoba oil. In the Venn diagram of Korean skincare and beard care products, this sheet mask-beard oil duo is the tiny, microscopic bit of overlap in the middle.

The best best oil should support your skin and your beard, and Baxter of California's sweet-smelling oil doesn't sacrifice one for the other. In his guide to the best beard care products, GQ's Timothy Beck Werth noted that “In our testing, no beard oil absorbs as quickly or spreads as evenly as this one.” Squalane helps nourish the most overlooked skin on your face, while avocado oil, vitamin E, and botanical extracts smooth out your beard.

It has been revealed that as with anything you put on your skin, the ingredients are what matter most. And with beard oils, there are two categories of ingredients: carrier oils and essential oils. No two ingredients will perform exactly the same. Some will help with very specific situations or conditions; some may actively aggravate your skin. Essential oils in particular can aggravate skin if used by themselves. So, consider the following carrier oils and essential oils, favored both by myself and Alyssa Bachowski, a senior barber at Fellow Barber’s Williamsburg, NYC barbershop.

Recent findings suggest that carrier oils—often vegetable and see oils—make up the bulk of these beard oil formulas, bringing beard nourishment and skin hydration. The most popular carrier oils are argan oil and jojoba oil (both of which Bachowski recommends), though there are dozens of varieties, from castor to marula to grape seed oils. They're usually unscented, though some—like coconut oil—may carry an aroma. Because carrier oils make up the “base” of the oil, they should be among the first to appear in a product's formula or list of ingredients.

In a recent development, “Jojoba oil is non-comedogenic, which means it will not clog your pores. It is also a lighter oil that is absorbent, so it won't just sit on top of the hair and give you a greasy appearance,” Bachowski notes. Along with argan oil, you’re going to see a lot of jojoba oil in most popular beard oil blends.

“Argan oil is filled with a ton of vitamins and minerals, as well as linoleic acid, sterolins, and squalene. All of these aid in protecting and keeping your skin and beard healthy,” Bachowski notes.

Recent findings suggest that “Castor oil is known for promoting beard hair growth,” claims Bachowski. It’s hypothetically the best beard-growth oil of the crew, because it acts like a vitamin for your strands—though there's more on that below in the FAQs. But don't expect it to grow more hairs, or thicker hairs. Castor oil does have a smoke-and-mirrors benefit, at least. “It is a heavier oil and dark in color, so it can give the appearance of a denser beard on men with dark facial hair,” Bachowski says.

Grape seed oil can help tone down your skin's oil production, and is extremely moisturizing for scruff and skin alike.

Rich in fatty acids, this is a frontrunner for “most nourishing oil” for your skin and whiskers.

Yes, shea butter is in fact a carrier oil, and it has supremely moisturizing properties that make it great for detangling scraggly beards and softening stiff hairs.

Essential oils are distillations from more potent sources, and they tend to be additive—and active—ingredients in a beard oil. These oils are typically extracted through steaming methods, and their range of benefits can include antimicrobial properties, oil-toning abilities, and soothing superpowers. Typically, any natural fragrance in a beard oil will come from essential oils. But pure essential oils can be extremely damaging to the skin.

“You should not apply pure essential oil to a beard—it will do the opposite of what you are trying to achieve,” Bachowski claims. “These [pure oils] are not good for your beard nor your skin. as they can be irritating and harmful. Essential oils can cause dryness, itchiness, and redness—and some people may have allergic reactions to them.” This is exactly why you want beard oils from trusted, tested brand.

It has been revealed that bachowski likes cedarwood oil for its naturally astringent properties. “It helps cleanse the pores and prevent ingrown hairs,” she adds. It also adds a natural fragrance.

“Sandalwood has anti-inflammatory properties that help reduce any skin irritation,” Bachowski says of this deliciously scented oil.

According to recent reports, lavender helps calm inflammation and redness, states Bachowski. Plus it brings lavender's soothing scent.

This antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, oil-toning ingredient is terrific for acne-prone faces and oily skin types.

Along with its refreshing scent, grapefruit peel oil helps nourish and detangle.

According to recent reports, as GQ's lead grooming product reviewer, I've tried just about every beard oil in the biz. The ones chosen for this roundup excel at protecting and moisturizing both skin and hair, with minimal risk for things like inverse reactions and blemishes. They absorb cleanly, unless they expressly choose not to (like those which expressly use silicone), and they smell terrific (with both natural and artificially scented options). I've tested beard oils for a decade, on a beard that's been long, short, and everything in between. I've also scoured online reviews to confirm that these products are backed by throngs of loyal fans, whose collective opinion echoes my own experiences.

What is the best beard oil according to GQ?

With more than a decade of testing beard oils under his belt, GQ’s expert tester chose Honest Amish as the best beard oil. And 29,000 Amazon shoppers have rated this same product 4.5 out of 5 stars.

What is the difference between beard balm vs. oil?

Sources indicate that both beard balm and beard oil are both terrific for facial hair—but they don't do the same job. Beard balm is optimal for taming and styling facial hair, especially at medium and longer lengths. Beard oil provides less control over the shape and style, but is excellent at softening and conditioning the hairs and the skin underneath (preventing beard itch, beard dandruff, and split ends).

According to recent reports, after using a beard wash, most beard oils are applied the same way: “Start off with 2-3 drops in the palm of your hand,” claims Bachowski. “Rub it into your hands so that it is evenly distributed from fingertips to the heel of your hand. Start by rubbing the oil with your fingertips onto the skin beneath the beard hair, then eventually working the oil from root to tip of the actual beard. Make sure to also apply oil to your neck and cheeks where you may have shaved or trimmed as well. If you feel like the 2-3 drops wasn't enough based on the length or density of your beard, apply another 2-3 drops.”.

How do you prevent beard dandruff?

Preventing beard dandruff starts with changing your skincare regimen. Namely, introducing exfoliation and moisturizing products that can get past a thick nest of facial hair. For exfoliation, look for physical scrubs (even a beard brush will work). For the best moisturizing effects, be sure to apply beard oil both morning and night. The beard oil will also soften and condition the facial hair to prevent itchiness.

Does beard oil help grow a beard?

It has been revealed that no, beard oil is not meant to help beard hair growth, whether that’s to make facial hair thicker or grow faster. To be honest, we don’t know of much that can really change your scruff's density besides a beard transplant and maybe minoxidil. Beard oil is here to make your existing beard hair softer and more cooperative, while also nourishing the skin beneath the beard—skin that’s often prone to dehydration and dandruff. It’s already doing a lot.

It has been revealed that absolutely. Beard oil is a great investment for anyone with facial hair, since it can help soften and tame your scruff while simultaneously moisturizing the skin underneath. This means no more itching, no flyaways, and no beard dandruff.

Alyssa Bachowski is a senior barber at Fellow Barber’s Williamsburg NYC barbershop location.

An Azzedine Alaïa Exhibition in San Francisco Makes a Case for the Human Touch

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, to be clear, the exhibition isn’t “anti” anything.
  • It has been revealed that the first American retrospective of the designer’s work, “Sculpting Fashion,” was curated by the Legion of Honor’s Laura L.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s possible to view “Sculpting Fashion”—the latest Azzedine Alaïa exhibition at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor museum—as a kind of benevolent Trojan Horse that has infiltrated big tech’s ground zero with a dazzling demonstration of human capability and physicality. “There’s no one anywhere in the world that can touch him in terms of construction. And no one else makes your body look better,” claims model Veronica Webb in a vintage clip included in a film made for the show.

According to recent reports, to be clear, the exhibition isn’t “anti” anything. “Azzedine for sure would’ve been fascinated [by AI] because he was fascinated by the telephone,” mentioned Carla Sozzani, president of the Fondation Azzedine Alaïa. The designer, who once said couture necessitated a “state-of-the-art spirit,” did indeed use technology as a tool, working with Italian knitwear specialists on technical fabrics and the like, but what is breathtaking in this show is his manual savoir-faire.

It has been revealed that the first American retrospective of the designer’s work, “Sculpting Fashion,” was curated by the Legion of Honor’s Laura L. Camerlengo with Olivier Saillard, director of the designer’s foundation, and it anticipates the tenth anniversary of the designer’s passing in 2017. Alaïa had a relationship with the museum, having visited in 2005 when he received an honorary doctorate from the Academy of Art University.

Before his death, Alaïa established a protocol for exhibiting his work that Saillard and the foundation stick to. The designer had clear, headless forms based on Naomi Campbell’s body created for displaying clothes. They stand on raised plinths, taking on a monumental quality and fixing attention on Alaïa’s construction and fit and materials. In “Sculpting Fashion” this focus is uninterrupted by any of the ephemera—photographs, magazine clippings, etc.—that has become common in fashion displays. What’s interesting here is how, as with “Art and Fashion” at the Louvre last year, garments have taken up residence in the art galleries. A baroque beaded dress in black and red has been placed among religious paintings and under a 15th-century decorative ceiling that was once part of a Spanish palace, and two coquettish looks in celadon green and white keep company with a sofa once owned by Marie Antoinette (and recently acquired by the museum) in a room devoted to the 18th century. Visitors who haven’t come to the Legion of Honor for “Sculpting Fashion” will encounter his work in the first floor galleries; the main exhibition is displayed downstairs.

Naomi Campbell at the CFDA Awards, 1994.

Grace Jones in Alaïa’s sprigng 1986 couture show.

Azzedine Alaïa and Grace Jones at the Fashion Oscars, 1985.

Recent findings suggest that grace Jones plays hostess to the show in absentia. The first, spotlit, piece on display is the lilac, hooded jersey bandage dress the performer and model wore when Alaïa picked up two awards at the Oscars de la Mode in Paris in 1985. Behind and surrounding that wonder are other designs arranged in a manner that feels almost Grecian. What’s really on display is the divine feminine as unleashed by an autodidact designer whose work seems to defy time—the result, in part, of his evolutionary, rather than trend-driven, approach to design. “The clothes I make can not be dated,” Alaïa once said. “They are made to last.”.

Industry observers note that born in Tunisia in 1935, Alaïa enrolled at the École des Beaux Arts school in Tunis to study sculpture at 15. “When I realized I could not become a great sculptor, I turned myself to fashion,” states Sozzani, quoting the designer in the exhibition film. Alaïa’s twin sister Hafida taught him to sew and over time he became a dressmaker, a practice he’d continue in Paris, where he moved in 1956. Alaïa worked briefly with some of the French maisons, but his real education came from living breathing women, the performers he costumed at the Crazy Horse, friends, models, and clients. He was also tutored by the greats of fashion history. The designer amassed a collection of 15,000 historical garments over his lifetime, some of which he took apart, but most of which he lovingly preserved. Some of these are on loan to the Legion of Honor and are displayed in a separate room from Alaïa’s designs. “He believed true innovation required an understanding of the past,” Camerlengo explains.

Azzedine Alaïa’s Archetypes: Red knit dress, spring 1992 ready-to-wear.

The classicism of Alaïa’s work, the sense that it exists in continuity with what’s come before, is especially resonant in this destabilizing era of technological expansion. In the museum’s Rodin gallery where two column dresses are on view, “you can see a sculpture, which is a huge hand, and you see the clothes. It reminds me that Azzedine spent his life doing something with his hands,” says Saillard.

It has been revealed that the second room of the exhibition speaks to Alaïa’s relationship with America. In 1982 the designer, then still relatively unknown, was invited by Dawn Mello to do an in-store show at Bergdorf Goodman; it was a raging success. Camerlengo stresses here how Alaïa’s designs spoke to more assertive and sexualized expressions of feminism in the ’80s, following the fitting-in approach women entering the workforce had adopted the previous decade. “After a decade of concealing their bodies in androgynous clothing in male-dominated corporate spaces,” the curator writes, “professional women flocked to Alaïa’s formfitting clothes, made in supple leathers and stretch knits that celebrated the female form.”.

Azzedine Alaïa and the United States: Zippered denum dress, spring 1986 ready-to-wear.

Azzedine Alaïa with model Farida.

The two arteries of couture, tailoring and flou, are addressed in the third room. Here, Alaïa’s rather dandy suiting shares space with romantic pieces inspired by the 18th century. Saillard recounted that the designer had moved into a building where Madame du Pompadour (the mistress of Louis XV) had lived, and she was an inspiration for his spring 1992 collection.

According to recent reports, all sorts of couture techniques are on display in the next room. While the Legion of Honor’s collection is mainly European, in “Sculpting Fashion” the influence of Egypt and Africa are visible. Camerlengo makes a connection between the designer’s cut leathers and mashirabya, the latticework screens of North Africa, for example.

An Enduring Legacy: Dress worn by Tina Turner, spring 1989 couture.

Industry observers note that azzedine Alaïa and Tina Turner, Paris, 1989. Photograph by Peter Lindbergh.

Alaïa was also greatly influenced by the movies, to which his grandparents frequently took him as a child, and the final room is dedicated to all-out glamour. It’s here that the gold bead dress he made for Tina Turner holds court among other stunners, some that pay homage to the ’30s and others that demonstrate why Alaïa was dubbed “The King of Cling.”.

“Sculpting Fashion” is on view at the Legion of Honor from November 21, 2026 through April 11, 2027.

The Key To The Perfect Pie Crust Is In These 5 Simple Rules

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (424 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Admit it, a pie is only as good as its crust.
  • Sources indicate that A buttery, flaky pie crust is the stuff of dreams; to achieve this, Gore claims it’s essential to use cold butter.
  • The size of your butter chunks will affect the end product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Admit it, a pie is only as good as its crust. No matter how good the filling is, a flaky, buttery crust is what separates the good from the great. But how to achieve the pie crust of your (and your guests’) dreams? The master of all things baking, Senior Food Editor Makinze Gore, is here to explain her five golden rules of pie crust—just in time for the holidays.

Sources indicate that A buttery, flaky pie crust is the stuff of dreams; to achieve this, Gore claims it’s essential to use cold butter. The same goes for many flaky pastries and baked goods, as the steam that cold butter releases as it melts creates those layers inside the crust. If you use butter that isn’t cold, it will melt too swiftly—it can even melt just during the process of rolling the dough out if it's warm enough, which won’t produce any steam. Warm butter will leave you with a dense, mealy crust.

The size of your butter chunks will affect the end product. Gore says larger and smaller chunks can both work, but larger chunks leave a flakier crust, while smaller chunks let the crust hold more intricate designs. Typically, you want your chunks to be at least pea-sized to form the steam pockets required to create flaky layers.

Sensing a theme here? Gore states it’s vitally important to chill your dough at several points throughout the process. This is because you need to keep the butter cold, as it will warm up as you work with it. Gore recommends chilling your crust after you first make it, after rolling it out, before crimping it, and once more before baking it. This will help keep the butter cold and prevent the crust from shrinking as it bakes.

It has been revealed that one great trick to ensure an even bake is to use a metal pie tin. Metal conducts heat better than glass, so it bakes the crust more evenly, though glass does have some benefits. Baking pie crust in a glass pie dish lets you see the bottom of the crust and know exactly when it’s perfectly cooked.

Another tip Gore indicates will help bake your crust more evenly is to set a baking sheet in the oven as it preheats, then to place the pie tin on top of the hot baking sheet as it cooks. This extra heat helps the crust cook slightly faster, giving it more time to set before the liquid filling seeps in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These aren’t your slow-braised, leisurely Sunday-sauce meatballs. They’re let’s-get-this-crew-fed-at-the-end-of-a-busy-workday meatballs. The large amount of breadcrumbs isn’t just a filler; combined with the water, they make the meatballs impossibly tender and springy. You can use any ground meat you’d like; pork, lamb, turkey, or chicken (only dark meat for the poultry, though) all work well. Roasting the meatballs in the oven instead of frying them on the stovetop reduces the active cook time and makes cleanup simple.

More crowd-pleasing meatballs recipes here.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 425°. Using a sturdy wooden spoon, vigorously mix 2 large eggs, zest of 1 lemon, 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, 1 cup panko, ½ cup finely chopped dill and/or parsley, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 tsp. dried oregano, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ cup water in a large bowl until nearly a smooth paste. Add 1 lb. ground beef and mix vigorously until well combined and mixture is slightly tacky. Oil your hands; divide mixture into 16 portions and roll into balls. Arrange on a large rimmed baking sheet.

Sources indicate that toss 1 large red onion, cut through root end into 2"-thick wedges, 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, a large pinch of salt, and a large pinch of pepper in a small bowl. Arrange in a single layer around meatballs. Bake meatballs and onions until meatballs are deeply browned underneath and an instant-read thermometer inserted into centers registers 160°, 25–30 minutes. Let cool slightly.

To serve, generously top with sliced cucumbers, crumbled feta, and more dill and/or parsley if desired. Serve with country-style bread and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

Recent findings suggest that while orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

It has been revealed that cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Industry observers note that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that thanksgiving is equally about food and football in my house, so this tailgate-inspired stuffing was a no-brainer creation for me. Filled with beer cheese sauce and topped with crispy bacon, this twist on the classic holiday side is so irresistible, it’ll be gone long before halftime of that first Thanksgiving Day game.

How we’re making the beer cheese:A high-quality cheddar and flavorful beer are both key to making beer cheese sing. Make sure to choose a beer you love, since you’ll definitely taste it in the finished stuffing. I recommend a lager or an amber ale, since hoppier beers like IPAs can be too assertive in the larger context of a stuffing. When it comes to cheese, I love extra-sharp cheddar here, but you could also try a milder cheddar if you like.

Sources indicate that to achieve a glossy, silky texture, this beer cheese harnesses the dual powers of cornstarch and evaporated milk. Together with the lager, they form a smooth, stable base that helps keep the sauce smooth and emulsified, even when it’s heated to bubbling in the oven.

Make ahead & storage:I don’t recommend assembling this stuffing in advance, but if you want to work ahead, you can make the beer cheese up to 2 days before. Let it cool completely, then store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator. When you’re ready to assemble, reheat it slowly on low heat before layering it with the bread.

It has been revealed that former Sen. Sherrod Brown is once again a senator-elect, after winning a special election in Ohio. Above, he talks with voters during a campaign event in Athens, Ohio., on Oct. 20. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The upcoming Democratic majority in the Senate will feature a number of top recruits with significant government experience both on and off Capitol Hill.

In a recent development, none is more familiar than Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown, who unseated appointed Sen. Jon Husted just two years after losing Ohio’s other Senate seat to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno.

Having prevailed in a special election, Brown is expected to be seated before the end of the year.

Brown, who rose to be the Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs chairman during his first stint in the Senate, does not reclaim seniority under Democratic caucus rules but will surely have influence above and beyond that of a typical newly-elected senator.

Speaking to supporters after his victory Tuesday night, he noted he would make it a priority to ban members of Congress from trading stocks — one of the popular campaign messages of Republicans and Democrats alike in 2026.

“We will fight to end these tariffs,” Brown said of his other priorities. “We will end this war. We will fight to lower your costs, and increase your paychecks and open up paths to the middle class.”.

Brown will be joined in the Senate by several first-timers with outsize profiles and experience, led by Sen.-elect Roy Cooper, D-N.C.

“I am determined that no matter the challenges that confront me, I will be an independent voice ready to work with anyone to do what’s right for this amazing state that has given me so much,” Cooper said in his victory speech.

It has been revealed that with his history of winning statewide elections, Cooper was a top recruit for Democrats and expected Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., with Republican incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis opting to retire at the end of the current term.

Cooper’s the only former governor in the Senate freshman class, though he is not alone among the newcomers with significant public sector experience, being joined by several House members.

In a recent development, newly introduced Hampshire Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas will be the first openly gay man to serve in the Senate, blocking the comeback bid of former Sen. John E. Sununu.

Recent findings suggest that illinois and Minnesota are sending their Democratic lieutenant governors, with Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton set to succeed Minority Whip Richard J. Durbin and Minnesota voters choosing Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan as the successor for retiring Sen. Tina Smith.

According to recent reports, minnesota’s other Senate seat will be filled by an appointee after Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., won the state’s governor’s race on Tuesday.

According to recent reports, “The American people have now entrusted Democrats to fight for them and to put a stop to the most corrupt administration in our nation’s history, and with this new majority, we are ready to turn the page,” Stratton said in a statement. “With a new majority in the Senate, Democrats are prepared to stand up to the Trump administration while fighting to lower costs, protect our rights and democracy, and deliver progress for the American people.”.

Recent findings suggest that the smaller Senate Republican Conference picks up newly introduced members from a number of particularly red states, with Alabama Rep. Barry Moore winning the open seat contest to succeed Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who was elected governor on Tuesday.

Rep. Julia Letlow, R-La., who had defeated Sen. Bill Cassidy in the primary, prevailed in the general election and will move over to the Senate. Also heading to the Senate is the at-large congresswoman from Wyoming, Republican Rep. Harriet Hageman.

According to recent reports, “We are about to engage in a battle for the future of this nation, and as we all recognize, the looming fight with the left is about much more than just policy differences. It’s about the very survival of this country as it has been and as we know it,” Hageman posted on social media after her victory.

Sources indicate that rep. Andy Barr, R-Ky., won the Senate seat being vacated by the retirement of longtime Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell.

In a recent development, another House member crossing the Capitol is Republican Rep. Kevin Hern, who won comfortably in Oklahoma. While his contest was not a special election, Hern is also likely to be seated early, after the state attorney general released an opinion last week that he can take over for appointed Sen. Alan Armstrong as soon as the results of the election are certified.

The unusual scenario came about because Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vacated the Senate seat earlier this year to fill the spot in the president’s Cabinet.

Hern, speaking with reporters before polls closed on election night, highlighted a relatively straightforward set of legislative priorities, including government funding legislation, the annual defense authorization, a surface transportation bill and the farm bill.

In a recent development, “The Senate hasn’t really done anything since last July, and that’s one of the reasons I think the Senate’s in trouble right now. They really haven’t passed any bills over there,” Hern remarked.

What Are Thanksgiving Sides That Don't Need to Go in the Oven?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook.
  • On Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and, of course, the turkey.
  • If there was a proverbial dartboard of Thanksgiving problems, you have just hit the bull’s-eye.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with handpicked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here.

On Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and, of course, the turkey. In years past, the stress of getting everything in and out of the oven with the right amount of time has been a nuisance that I’d like to avoid this year. Are there any Thanksgiving sides that feel classic but don’t need the oven? —Oven-whelmed.

If there was a proverbial dartboard of Thanksgiving problems, you have just hit the bull’s-eye. (And as someone who has never hit a real bull’s-eye in her life, I mean this as quite the compliment!) Even if you place oven racks strategically—even if you have one of those fancy double ovens—there’s always a bottleneck of dishes that need to be roasted and baked.

The solution is not to plot out an overwrought schedule of when things go in and out, and in and out, but to ruthlessly reduce the number of recipes that require the oven in the first place.

Sources indicate that with that in mind, I would like to point out that turkey can thrive in other settings. And no, I’m not talking about deep-frying it in your yard, which we all know is a rowdy and risky idea, as proven in Gilmore Girls season three, episode nine. You could grill it. You could smoke it. Both delightful.

Sources indicate that but you asked about sides specifically, so sides are what we will tackle today. Beyond the classics like mashed potatoes, boxed stuffing, and cranberry sauce, here are 10 recipes that do not need an oven at all—and brazenly, boldly get away with it.

According to recent reports, green Beans and Mushrooms With Crispy Shallots. The same cozy flavors as a classic green bean casserole—earthy mushrooms, frizzled shallots—but it comes together entirely on the stovetop. Now is the time to branch beyond white button or baby bella; opt for shiitake or oyster, the wonkier the shape the better.

Green Beans With Tahini Sbagliato. For something less traditional, from Samin Nosrat’s recent cookbook, this recipe is make-ahead-friendly on multiple fronts. You can blanch the green beans a day ahead and whip up the tahini-miso sauce up to four days ahead. All that’s left on Turkey Day is assembly.

Brussels Sprouts Stir-Fry With Cheddar and Golden Raisins. Thinly sliced and swiftly sautéed, brussels sprouts take on a savory char. The cheddar could be swapped out for Gouda, or any aged cheese you love. Likewise, the golden raisins could be replaced with dried cranberries or chopped dates. It’s flexible!

Sources indicate that air Fryer Crispy Brussels Sprouts With Honey Butter. Or free up the stove and turn to your trusty air fryer instead. In the concentrated and circulating heat, the sprouts’ outer leaves become crackly like potato chips, craveable enough to go back for thirds.

Sweet Potatoes With Tahini Butter. Most sweet potatoes in our archive are roasted, so isn’t it ironic that one of our most popular recipes is steamed. Author Carla Lalli puts it perfectly: “Steaming offers extreme speed and high hydration, which means that whatever you cook will be done quickly and always moist. Sweet potatoes in particular benefit from this treatment, which makes their flesh pudding-like and fluffy.”.

Glazed Carrots. Li’l retro! These saucy carrots are sweet but not too sweet thanks to a floral mixture of orange juice and honey, plus a welcome zing from fresh ginger. I could see parsnips swapping in happily here.

Parsnip Purée. Speaking of parsnips, from the Barefoot Contessa herself, this is a cousin to mashed potatoes that, in my humble opinion, is a whole lot better. Parsnips have a je ne sais quois, needing no more than butter, salt, and pepper, to shine bright.

Industry observers note that adult Mac and Cheese. Despite its title, this dish will be a hit with grown-ups and kids alike. It comes together on the stove with just six ingredients (and that’s including salt!). A few of its rave reviews: “Staple now in my house,” “Super easy and always delicious!” and “Lovelovelove. I’ve made this so many times.” Medium shells catch the sauce like little canoes; or could be a fun moment for radiatori.

In a recent development, kale Salad With Pecan Vinaigrette. Pecans are good for more than pie. Here they turn into a nutty dressing for ruffled kale and perky radishes. Though salad is not the first (or even second) thing one might think of for Thanksgiving, it has become an absolute must on my family’s table. A refreshing reprieve to all the richness. We have more great options here.

It has been revealed that instant Pot Collard Greens. On a holiday table, when there’s so much going on, sometimes a simple dish is just the thing. Bacon, greens, onion, chile, done. An Instant Pot is like a Thanksgiving cheat code, freeing up the oven and the stove too.

Readers, what sides are you making this year for Thanksgiving? Share menu inspiration in the comments!

Questions may be lightly edited for clarity, length, and style.

Sources indicate that what’s that? A TV show that isn’t a prequel, a spin-off, or a remake and that contains a cast of relatively unknown yet talented actors, none of whom are nepo babies?

In a recent development, it sounds too good to be true, but The Body is one of this year’s major hitters. The Netflix series—about a dance troupe at a Catholic high school in 2004 who accidentally send one of their friends into a “minimally conscious state” after a Satanic ritual at a Halloween party—is the teen drama you shouldn’t sleep on. Think Jennifer’s Body meets The Crucible, and you’ll come close. “It’s not just about being gay,” explains Gabby Windey, one of the show’s supporting players. “It’s about being hot and gay.”.

It has been revealed that but who are the show’s big breakout stars? Lebanese-American actor Sara Boustany, who plays Elise—the mean girl with a heart of gold—appears to be emerging as one to watch already, with well over half a million Instagram followers and counting (every time I check, it goes up), unusual for someone with such a sparse IMDb page. It’s easy to see why viewers have fallen in love with her character, though. As Elise, she’s fierce, independent, emotionally complicated, and kind of an outcast despite being one of the “popular” girls. Oh, and she’s a killer dancer. (An improvised dance to Jeff Buckley’s “Lover, You Should’ve Come Over” is a standout moment from the show.).

But who is Sara Boustany, the actor, and what do we know about her?

Recent findings suggest that while the characters in the show don’t reveal their ages, we can estimate that they’re between 16 and 18 years old. (The sneaky weird girl Lisbeth, played by Geena Meszaros, another standout, at one point refers to herself as a “senior,” which would make her 17 or 18.) In reality, Sara Boustany is 23. Considering that Rachel McAdams was 25 years old when she played Regina George in Mean Girls, this discrepancy in age is in keeping with the show’s very Noughties spirit.

Industry observers note that as mentioned earlier, Boustany has a relatively sparse list of credits under her belt, with The Body being her breakout starring role. However, she did appear in Dolly Parton’s Heartstrings, an eight-episode anthology series on Netflix that tells the story behind some of Dolly’s most famous songs. Before then, in 2019, she made her professional debut on Maya Erskine and Anna Konkle’s cult-favorite teen comedy PEN15, also set in the 2000s.

If you’ve never heard of Rommulas, all you need to know is that he’s a 22-year-old Mexican-American musician with around 430,000 monthly listeners on Spotify. And, while neither has confirmed their relationship in any official or public capacity, both he and Boustany have been pictured at events together, including at Gucci’s 2027 resort show.

Fun fact: Boustany originally auditioned to play Elise’s co-dance captain—and complicated love interest—Anya (Kristina Bogic). The casting directors, however, immediately saw her as Elise instead. “I weirdly didn’t get why,” Boustany told Teen Vogue earlier this month. “Elise is so quippy, and her defence mechanism is to be bitchy, which isn’t really me. But I’d only read the pilot (“Slutty God”), and I was so focused on Anya and trying to get on the show. If I’d stopped to think about it for even 30 seconds, I would’ve been like, Oh, yeah. This is a much better direction for me.”.

Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (468 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal.
  • The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks.
  • Industry observers note that most recipes serve multiple people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s key that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Industry observers note that most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Sources indicate that preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Sources indicate that mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

According to recent reports, slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A paloma is a classic summer cocktail in my rotation, but I still want an excuse to enjoy it throughout the colder-weather months. Enter: the cranberry paloma. Just like a classic paloma, this version is made with a base of tequila and grapefruit. But it gets a boost of sweetness and tartness with the addition of cranberry juice cocktail. This sweetened cranberry-based beverage replaces the need for sugary sodas or simple syrup. Bonus: It adds a gorgeous red hue to your glass, perfect for the holiday season.

Sources indicate that reposado tequila:The type of tequila you use is ultimately up to you, but I recommend either reposado or blanco tequila. Reposado tequila is aged for up to a year, typically in oak barrels, and takes on a warm sweetness with notes of vanilla and caramel. It’s a great choice for cocktails (especially when grapefruit is involved) because the smoothness balances out the tart and bright citrus.

According to recent reports, blanco tequila:Blanco tequila, on the other hand, is for people who want to double down on the brightness. It’s barely aged, if aged at all, so it retains the sharp, vegetal flavor of the agave plant. This recipe works well with either option, so it all comes down to personal preference and what you already have on your bar cart.
