How to Blind-Bake Pie Crust—and When You Need To

📅 16 May 2016 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1430 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the road to pie perfection is paved in pitfalls.
  • Industry observers note that but getting the crust to the right color depends on what you’re planning to fill it with.
  • Industry observers note that blind baking is especially useful when the filling needs less time in the oven than the crust does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the road to pie perfection is paved in pitfalls. I’ve fallen into plenty of them throughout my baking career. The infamous “soggy bottom” is among the most common, but it’s easy to avoid. Blind baking—baking the crust before adding the filling—helps prevent an underbaked crust by giving the pastry a head start in the oven or cooking it completely before the filling goes in.

Industry observers note that but getting the crust to the right color depends on what you’re planning to fill it with. A pale, partially baked shell might be perfect for one pie, while another needs a deep golden brown crust before you add even a spoonful of filling. Here’s how to know when enough color is enough.

Industry observers note that blind baking is especially useful when the filling needs less time in the oven than the crust does. For custard pies, like pumpkin pie, partially baking the shell gives the pastry a head start so it doesn’t end up uncooked beneath a set filling. For pies with no-bake fillings, such as chocolate pudding pie or cranberry curd pie, the crust needs to be fully baked before it’s filled.

Most traditional fruit pies don’t need blind baking. Their fillings and crusts spend enough time in the oven together for the pastry to cook through. There are exceptions, particularly single-crust fruit pies topped with a crumble. Our Peach-Blueberry Pie, for example, starts with a thoroughly blind-baked shell before the filling goes in. Follow your recipe’s instructions rather than assuming every fruit pie needs the same treatment.

Recent findings suggest that start with a good pie dough. Roll it out, fit it into the pie plate, and crimp the edge. Chill the shaped shell for at least 15 minutes before baking; cold dough holds its shape better in the oven, reducing the risk of shrinking or slumping.

Next, line the shell with parchment paper and fill it with pie weights. Crumpling the parchment first, then unfolding it, helps it conform to the shell. The weights hold the dough against the pan while it bakes, preventing the bottom from puffing up and the sides from collapsing.

You can buy ceramic pie weights or use dried beans, rice, or stainless-steel ball bearings. I’m partial to the ball bearings: They’re small enough to settle into the corners of the pie plate and heavy enough to hold the dough firmly in place.

Not everyone in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen agrees. Editors Jesse Szewczyk and Rebecca Firkser prefer lighter alternatives. In their experience, heavy metal weights can compress the dough, limiting the expansion of the buttery layers that make pie crust flaky. Jesse uses dried beans or rice; Rebecca prefers dried chickpeas or even granulated sugar, a technique popularized by baking expert Stella Parks.

In a recent development, all of these options can work. Whichever you choose, fill the parchment-lined shell generously, supporting the sides all the way to the rim. Leave the weights in place until the crust looks dry and set and the parchment releases easily; removing them too soon can cause the sides to slump.

Our Cranberry Meringue Pie has a fully blind-baked pie crust.

This method uses our Perfect Pie Crust dough and makes one 9"-diameter pie shell. It produces an evenly golden crust; if your pie calls for a paler or more deeply browned shell, follow its specific baking instructions and use the visual guide below.

Recent findings suggest that some pie recipes call for docking (pricking the bottom and sides of the dough with a fork) before baking. This allows steam to escape and helps prevent uneven puffing, but doesn’t replace the support of pie weights. Follow your recipe’s instructions; docking isn’t necessary for every blind-baked crust.

In a recent development, do Ahead: A fully blind-baked crust can be made up to 2 days ahead. Let cool completely, wrap well, and store at room temperature until ready to fill.

The short answer: It depends on what you’re putting inside. Some pies need only a partially baked crust, while others call for a shell that’s deeply golden brown.

Oven temperatures vary, different pie plates conduct heat differently, and the filling determines how much additional baking the crust will get. Use the recipe’s timing as a guide, but watch the color and texture of the pastry. Here’s what to look for.

In a recent development, fruit pies need a pale base because they bake a looong time. Or at least, that’s often the thinking. If you’re making a single-crust variety topped with a crumble, such as our Blueberry Crumble Pie, and the recipe calls for blind-baking, you might want to start with an anemic crust. It’ll have plenty of time to brown as the juices thicken.

A pale, partially baked crust should look set rather than raw. The bottom should look set and opaque with some light golden patches, while the crimped edge may already be noticeably browned. The crust will continue to develop color once the filling goes in.

Don’t assume fruit pies always need a pale shell. Our Peach-Blueberry Pie, for example, calls for a well-browned crust before the fruit and crumble go in. And many double-crust fruit pies don’t need blind baking at all.

Sources indicate that A lightly baked shell can also be appropriate for custards that have a substantial bake ahead. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie starts with a partially baked crust before the custard goes in for at least another hour.

The goal is to give the crust enough of a head start without taking it so far that the edges burn before the filling finishes cooking.

Custard pies, such as chess and our Lemon Buttermilk Pie, often have shorter bake times than fruit pies, so the crust needs a solid golden base layer to develop enough color by the time the filling sets.

Here, you’re looking for more than a crust that’s simply dry and set. The bottom should be evenly golden with no pale, translucent patches, and the sides should have taken on some color too. The rim will generally be a little darker than the bottom, but the whole shell should look well on its way to being fully baked.

Our Perfect Pie Crust recipe produces this kind of shell. It calls for baking the weighted crust until the edges are golden, then removing the weights and continuing until the bottom and sides are evenly browned.

And some pies need an even more substantial head start. Our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie takes the crust to a dry golden finish before adding a filling that bakes for another 45–55 minutes.

In a recent development, the point isn’t that every custard pie needs the same color. It’s that the crust should be baked far enough that it won’t be left pale and doughy by the time the filling is done.

In a recent development, bake the crust to a dark golden brown if you’re adding a no-bake filling, like a pudding or curd. You’re going for a toasty, burnished color, so don’t be gun-shy.

Because the filling won’t return to the oven, this is the crust’s one chance to bake all the way through. You want deep color across the entire bottom and up the sides—not just a dark rim surrounding a pale center. The pastry should look dry, crisp, and well browned, without any doughy or translucent spots.

Recent findings suggest that after removing the pie weights, continue baking until the shell is fully browned, checking frequently toward the end. Depending on the dough and oven temperature, that might take another 15–20 minutes or longer. Don’t pull it simply because the timer has gone off.

Our Cranberry Meringue Pie uses this approach: The crust is baked until golden and dry before the cranberry curd filling goes in. A fully baked shell develops a richer, toastier flavor and is better equipped to stand up to a moist filling.

Some recipes, including our pumpkin pie, call for brushing a thin layer of beaten egg onto the partially baked shell and returning it to the oven briefly to set. This, ostensibly, creates a barrier between the pastry and the filling, but not all bakers believe the hype.

While it can be a useful extra precaution, it is by no means a universal requirement. If your recipe doesn’t call for it, there’s no need to add another step.

They’ll be here whenever you need them.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A sweeping tide of Democratic wins Tuesday left Republicans preparing for a new face atop the House GOP leadership ranks as the party gears up to defend President Donald Trump from a list of investigations.
  • It’s shaping up to be a battle between sitting Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, pitting two lawmakers Trump has publicly praised against one another.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, left, is seen in a House Republican Conference speaker election meeting on Oct. 13, 2023. Now he has his eyes on the minority leader post for the next Congress. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A sweeping tide of Democratic wins Tuesday left Republicans preparing for a new face atop the House GOP leadership ranks as the party gears up to defend President Donald Trump from a list of investigations.

It’s shaping up to be a battle between sitting Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, pitting two lawmakers Trump has publicly praised against one another.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana had been trying to stay the course before Republicans dropped a stunning amount of seats, including ones considered deep-red. The cascade of losses, which will give Democrats a sizable majority in the 435-member chamber, forced Johnson to stand down. He told his staff on a Wednesday morning call he would not seek the minority leader job for the next Congress when the GOP conference votes behind closed doors next week.

In a possible sign of what’s to come when the often-raucous conference meets to hear from candidates and vote, some GOP insiders were split Wednesday on which lawmaker should take over as leader.

Industry observers note that “It might be Jordan’s for the taking. I think the real fight will be at whip and conference chair,” stated one GOP source with ties to each member’s office, granted anonymity to be candid.

In a letter to colleagues Jordan circulated Wednesday, he pitched himself as “battle-tested on the oversight front,” which could help as Democrats go full-tilt on probing the Trump administration. “For too long, we have operated without a clear strategy to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democrat majority,” Jordan’s letter reads.

It has been revealed that but another person familiar with Scalise’s thinking said “his No. 1 goal will be to lead the conference back into the majority,” describing Scalise as a “proven and tested leader who is ready on day one.”.

“The conference knows him, how he fights, and that he’s a trusted leader,” the person said.

Spokespersons for Scalise and Johnson did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment on their plans.

Industry observers note that heading into the midterms, it appeared Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the sitting majority whip, had been working behind the scenes to shore up his standing with House GOP members in a bid to become the No. 2 Republican in January.

Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger of Texas has also pitched himself for minority whip, writing in a Wednesday letter to colleagues that he believed his conference needed “fresh ideas” and had “missed many opportunities.”.

Sources indicate that the scope of Tuesday’s losses had some calling for a completely clean slate, with Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., posting a message on social media to House and Senate brass: “Please do us all a favor and step aside so fresh leadership can take a truly conservative direction.”.

It has been revealed that “Having Jordan and Emmer in as leadership won’t be much of a change at the top,” the first GOP source remarked. “But President Trump should want a warrior like Jordan with impeachment experience in charge, given the Democrats will inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”.

It has been revealed that to that end, Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, likely the incoming House Judiciary Committee chairman, said in a brief interview before the chamber adjourned in September to campaign that “there’s a long list of potentially impeachable offenses” to look at from the president, his family members and inner circle.

An aggressive investigatory push by Democrats could make Jordan, in Trump’s eyes, an attractive candidate to lead the conference. Jordan fought hard against Trump’s two first-term impeachments, including with fiery cable news hits that were praised by the TV-focused chief executive.

Whatever happens, it will cap off a rocky ride for Johnson, who claimed the gavel in the tumultuous weeks after Kevin McCarthy was ousted as speaker in October 2023.

In a statement released early Wednesday morning, Johnson did not reveal his next move.

In a recent development, “While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning. This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history,” Johnson said. “However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world.”.

Notably, during a phone interview with Politico late Tuesday night, Trump was asked about Johnson — but did not endorse him for minority leader.

According to recent reports, “I think he’s done a very good job,” the president said, his voice hoarse from an October-long rally blitz that did not pay off for his party. “I mean, they’re going to have to make that decision. He’s going to have to make that decision. But he’s a good person and a good man.”.

On Wednesday Trump told reporters at the White House he intended to stay out of the coming House GOP leadership race.

While Republicans are eager to avoid repeating the bitter public battles of the past, the fight for minority leader is in some ways a rerun. Both Scalise and Jordan tried for the speaker’s gavel back in 2023 after McCarthy’s sacking but neither landed the job.

A former high school and college wrestler who later coached grappling, Jordan was once considered too much of a firebrand to lead the entire caucus.

Recent findings suggest that “Early on he wasn’t really given the opportunity to show what he’s capable of because of his steadfast conservative positions,” Ray Yonkura, who was Jordan’s chief of staff for a decade and has done political work for him, told CQ Roll Call in October 2023. “He was oftentimes pushed to the side, or different Republican leaders tried to keep him down.”.

“Once he was given an opportunity to show what he’s capable of, I think a lot of people realized that this is somebody whose skill set can actually be good in a leadership role,” Yonkura stated then.

Jordan has faced questions over the years about what he knew about sexual abuse by a doctor at The Ohio State University when he worked there as an assistant wrestling coach starting in the 1980s. He has repeatedly denied knowing of the abuse, and multiple Republicans told CQ Roll Call in 2023 that it hadn’t factored into their support for Jordan.

As for Scalise, he went through a public ordeal in 2017 when he was shot by a gunman at a GOP baseball practice, sustaining serious injuries. He later was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, and in 2024 remarked he was in remission.

According to recent reports, beyond the House leadership shuffle ahead of the start of the 120th Congress, G. William Hoagland, a former Senate GOP leadership aide, mentioned there would be a broader battle among Republicans as they analyze their losses and look ahead to 2028.

“I take Steve Bannon’s comment recently seriously that the Republican Party will be engulfed in a civil war over the future of the party,” he said, referring to recent comments from Trump’s former chief 2016 campaign and White House strategist. “Expect that civil war to play out over the next couple of weeks in the midst of all the other legislative complications they have to deal with in the lame-duck session.”.

Niels Lesniewski, Savannah Behrmann, Paul Krawczak and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—substantial, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

According to recent reports, making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Industry observers note that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling).

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Recent findings suggest that whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Recent findings suggest that place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Sources indicate that place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

According to recent reports, pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

Industry observers note that to serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

Industry observers note that CARRANCA draws on the eponymous sculptures, anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figures traditionally believed to ward off evil spirits, also associated with Afro-Brazilian religious traditions such as Candomblé. The project references Exu, the orisha who mediates between the material and spiritual worlds and is associated with movement and the creation of possibilities. Inspired by ancient Egyptian and Yoruba cultures, the carrancas’ physiognomy blends human and animal traits, evoking pre-dynastic Egyptian deities.

Industry observers note that the palette of black, red, indigo, and white references these traditions and Brazilian popular representations of Exu. Using Afro-surrealism as a conceptual framework, the series visually narrates Urias’ eponymous album, with each photograph corresponding to a track. The project explores transcorporeality and how reclaiming divine and ancestral figures can become a means of liberation from Eurocentric identity norms.

Creative Director, Art Director and Stylist: OdePhotography: MaltoniSet Design: Jean LabancaHair and Makeup: Ivan BarriaUrias’ Hair: Rafaella SchlinUrias’ Makeup: Camila AnacNail Artist: CyshimiProduction: BELTRAME+Post-Production: Studio Bruno RezendeCast: Fina Cadjancu, Akin Henrias and Marcinha do Corintho.

Ode (b. 1998) is a Brazilian multidisciplinary artist working across filmmaking, creative direction, styling, writing, and curatorial practice. Her work explores self-representation as a means of challenging Eurocentric notions of identity through transcorporeality, Afro-Brazilian spirituality, memory, and transformation. Her photobooks and films, including A Rose and A Prayer (2022), Divina (2022), and CARRANCA (2025), bring human figures, deities, and Afro-surrealist narratives into dialogue. Her work has been exhibited at MEP, Instituto Moreira Salles, Lafayette Anticipations, ICA London, Photo London, and SP-Arte. She founded the platform Dúdús (2016–2019) and has curated exhibitions dedicated to Afro-diasporic art. Her work has been featured in Vogue, Dazed, ArtReview, and Harper’s Bazaar, and she has collaborated with Comme des Garçons, Jean Paul Gaultier, and COLORSxSTUDIOS.

BA's Best Pecan Pie

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our classic pecan pie recipe has no chocolate chips, no booze, and no hard-to-find ingredients.
  • Sources indicate that brown sugar and a spoonful of dark molasses add depth to the filling, while toasting the pecans before incorporating them makes their flavor stand out and their texture more robust.
  • Recent findings suggest that when the pie comes out of the oven, the edges should be set and slightly puffed, but the center should still wobble like Jell-O.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our classic pecan pie recipe has no chocolate chips, no booze, and no hard-to-find ingredients. Instead of focusing on embellishments, we focused on what matters most: the deep flavor of toasted pecans, a caramelly custard, and a buttery, flaky pie crust.

Sources indicate that brown sugar and a spoonful of dark molasses add depth to the filling, while toasting the pecans before incorporating them makes their flavor stand out and their texture more robust. Blind baking the crust—baking it before adding the filling—helps keep the bottom crisp beneath the gooey custard.

Recent findings suggest that when the pie comes out of the oven, the edges should be set and slightly puffed, but the center should still wobble like Jell-O. It will continue to set as it cools, so resist slicing too soon. Serve it all on its own, or gild it with vanilla ice cream or whipped cream.

Can I make this pecan pie without corn syrup?

It has been revealed that yes. Corn syrup gives this classic pie its perfectly gooey texture, but there are alternatives. Brown rice syrup will add a toasty flavor and can be used in equal parts. Golden syrup, honey, and maple syrup are all too sweet and will change the pie’s flavor and texture.

For a pie developed without any syrup, try our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie.

Can I use chopped pecans instead of halves?

Yes. We love the crunch you get from pecan halves, but if you’re a chopped pecan person, use about 225 g in place of the 2 cups of halves. Watch closely when toasting; chopped pecans will need less time in the oven.

Can I make pecan pie ahead of time?

Yes—bake the pie a day ahead and refrigerate it. Let it cool on a rack for up to 2 hours, then transfer it to the refrigerator to finish cooling before covering. To get a head start on the pastry, refrigerate the dough for up to 3 days or freeze it for up to 2 months.

Pulse 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 2 cups all-purpose flour in a food processor until combined. Add 5 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 3 Tbsp. chilled lard or vegetable shortening and pulse until mixture resembles coarse meal with a few pieces of butter and lard visible, about fifteen 1-second pulses. With motor running, drizzle in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar and 5½ Tbsp. ice water and pulse until dough is still crumbly but just holds together when squeezed (add 1 tsp. water at a time if necessary, but be careful not to overwork dough).

Recent findings suggest that turn out dough onto a work surface. Knead 1–2 times, pressing just to incorporate any shaggy pieces. Flatten into a 6"-wide disk. Wrap with plastic wrap and chill at least 1 hour.

It has been revealed that preheat oven to 425°. Roll out dough on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie pan. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to lightly brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Bake until crust is set and beginning to brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool.

According to recent reports, do Ahead: Dough can be made 3 days ahead; keep chilled, or freeze up to 2 months. Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature.

According to recent reports, preheat oven to 350°. Toast 2 cups (225 g) pecan halves on a rimmed baking sheet until browned and fragrant, 8–10 minutes. Let cool.

According to recent reports, reduce oven temperature to 325°. Whisk 4 large eggs, room temperature, beaten to blend, 1 cup light corn syrup, ⅔ cup (packed; 134 g) light brown sugar, 1 Tbsp. robust-flavored (dark) molasses, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Slowly whisk in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, until combined. Fold in pecans and pour into cooled crust.

Bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 55–70 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with vanilla ice cream.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature.

Vogue First! Dagmar’s Pre-Spring Collection Lands Early on Net-a-Porter

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opening a boutique is a delicate exercise in materials and mood to bring its world to life in a physical space.
  • “When Rachel and I started to look at what the collection should be, we looked at our store,” Wallenstam shares with Vogue.
  • Recent findings suggest that launching November 19 alongside a new brand identity, the 130-piece pre-spring collection spans relaxed denim (a favorite of Wallenstam’s), sharp-shouldered tailoring, a croc pencil skirt, open-cut tanks, suede outerwear, and boots, much of it drawing on the textures and tones of the store.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opening a boutique is a delicate exercise in materials and mood to bring its world to life in a physical space. So it makes sense that for Karin Soderlind, Kristina Tjader, and Sofia Wallenstam, the sisters and founders behind Stockholm-based Dagmar, their Alyssa Kapito-designed flagship became a strong point of reference. When Wallenstam, the brand’s creative director, went looking for inspiration for pre-spring ‘27, the debut collection from new design director Rachael Proud, formerly creative director of Raey, the two didn’t need to look further than the walls of its new shop.

“When Rachel and I started to look at what the collection should be, we looked at our store,” Wallenstam shares with Vogue. In the flagship, a metal Jean Prouvé piece hangs on the wall alongside a handcrafted André Sornay sofa, and the tension between the two became the collection’s throughline. “The Prouvé piece on the wall is metal, quite hard, almost brutalist, and then we have this beautiful soft boucle sofa,” she claims. “That was the meeting point, the hard versus the soft.”.

Recent findings suggest that launching November 19 alongside a new brand identity, the 130-piece pre-spring collection spans relaxed denim (a favorite of Wallenstam’s), sharp-shouldered tailoring, a croc pencil skirt, open-cut tanks, suede outerwear, and boots, much of it drawing on the textures and tones of the store. “We wanted to reuse the bouclé, not in the same way obviously, but that feeling of it,” Wallenstam says. The colors, too—the blacks, whites, and browns—feel representative of the Dagmar woman, Wallenstam adds.

The collection also marks a latest chapter for the Dagmar woman, who Wallenstam describes as confident and living a busy, bustling life with a packed calendar. “She might go and have a school drop-off and go straight to a meeting, and then meet friends, go to a dinner,” she shares. “She wants to look smart and she wants to look cool at the same time.” With Proud on board, that approach is getting a little more edge, with roomier silhouettes and sharper shoulders at the forefront. It’s a bit more oversized than Dagmar has done in the past, with warmer tones integrated throughout. Wallenstam also pushes back on the notion of minimalism, so often pinned on Scandinavian fashion. “Of course, we have neutral tones, but it has heritage. It has a depth to it and a warmth to it.”.

Sources indicate that as for how she and Proud approached the collection together, “When Rachel and I first sat down to discuss what the collection should be and how it should feel, we started immediately with the Dagmar woman and what’s important to her,” Wallenstam states. And the pencil skirt is where Proud’s influence really demonstrates. “You can really see the meeting point between Rachel and Dagmar in the pencil skirt,” she says. “It’s a very feminine product, but it has an elastic waist to make it more relaxed, and it’s in croco, which is a little bit harder in the material.” It’s the piece in the collection that will feel as comfortable at your desk as it does at dinner—a full expression of the newly introduced Dagmar approach. It’s the Prouvé and the bouclé sofa all over again, translated into a single skirt. And of course, the same push and pull runs through the rest of the collection.

Prices range from $140 to $3,300, and Vogue readers can exclusively shop the collection on Dagmar for 24 hours, before its official launch on November 20; retailer drops on Net-a-Porter and Nordstrom to follow.

It has been revealed that as Democrats look ahead to their fresh Senate majority for the next Congress, their current leader Charles E. Schumer made a prediction on Wednesday: “I’ll be reelected as majority leader.”.

Schumer, a Democrat from Fresh York, would be helming a larger caucus than most anticipated, ranging from 54 to 56 seats after the dust settles from Tuesday’s wins.

Recent findings suggest that not all the new incoming members say they will support the 75-year-old, and some have called for new blood. But so far, no formidable opponent has emerged.

“The issue is not me,” Schumer told reporters outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Wednesday morning when asked about working with those new senators. “The issue is focusing on the American people and what they want.”.

The leadership election for Senate Democrats will likely take place in early December and include the senators-elect in a secret ballot race.

Industry observers note that minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who won a Senate election against Republican Michele Tafoya, told NBC’s Meet the Press NOW in August, “I think it is time for new leadership,” when asked if she’d support Schumer.

She reupped that sentiment on a Wednesday press call, saying, “Many of us were elected who refused corporate PAC money, who are beholden only to the people who elected us, and are ready to fight for bold change. And so I think it’s time for new leadership.”.

It has been revealed that schumer has served in both the minority and majority as Democratic leader after landing the job in 2017 when then-leader Harry Reid retired. He faces reelection in 2028.

Former state Senate President Troy Jackson of Maine, the Democrat who defeated Republican Sen. Susan Collins in her bid for a sixth term, told reporters on Monday, “I’ve already remarked that I told Sen. Schumer that I’m gonna support somebody else. It’s no different now.”.

He stated he would push Schumer to deliver on health care changes like “Medicare for All.”.

Sources indicate that democratic Rep. Chris Pappas of Latest Hampshire, who bested John Sununu in his bid to return to the Senate, stated in an interview last week that “it’s very clear voters are hungry for new voices at the table and for a new generation of leadership in the Senate.”.

Sources indicate that “I’ve heard that throughout this campaign. I think above all, people want folks who understand the challenges out there and are going to fight with the urgency that these challenges deserve,” he mentioned. “Too often, we’ve seen leadership flat-footed.”.

His campaign did not immediately respond to questions Wednesday about whether that was indicative of his support for Schumer.

Recent findings suggest that democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist church who unseated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, told CNN in September: “I’m not supporting Schumer for leader.”.

“I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer, but we need fresh leadership. We need new, younger leadership, young blood. I don’t mean just age, but people who are bringing fresh ideas and fresh leadership,” he mentioned. “We’ve got to have leaders that can unite us, bring us together. Not just Democrats, but bring together Democrats and Republicans to solve real problems.”.

“I think people are frustrated with the gridlock and the sense that people are not working together,” he added, pointing to Democrats blocking the farm bill in the Senate Agriculture Committee earlier this year.

It has been revealed that abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan, told MS NOW earlier this fall he would want to support Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen as leader.

It has been revealed that “I would definitely support Sen. Chris Van Hollen and I would love to see him as Senate majority leader,” he said.

Van Hollen is seen as a presidential contender, and has been “kicking the tires” on 2028 instead of Senate leadership when he’s been asked.

In a recent development, el-Sayed told NBC’s Today Show on Wednesday, just hours after his race was called, “We need action. We need leadership toward that action. I’m interested to see, working with our caucus, to see what options we’ve got,” saying he hopes there is “two or more options” but not mentioning Van Hollen.

“I’m going to vote for the option that gives me the best chance at getting money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All,” he remarked.

Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton made it part of her Senate primary pitch earlier this year that she was the only Democrat in the race who didn’t support Schumer. “I’ve made it clear that I would not support Chuck Schumer as leader of the Democratic caucus because I think right now what I’m hearing from voters all across the state of Illinois is that they are fed up. They’re fed up with what’s happening in Washington,” she told political YouTube commentator Jack Cocchiarella in March.

A spokesperson for Stratton’s campaign reiterated Wednesday her position hasn’t changed. The campaigns of El-Sayed, Hamilton and Jackson did not immediately respond to questions Wednesday about their stances.

Even if some candidates were eager to distance themselves from establishment Democrats on the campaign trail before facing voters, it’s hard to deny that Schumer helped bring home a resounding victory for Democrats on Tuesday night.

So far, among Democratic incumbents, it’s not clear anyone would have the appetite to challenge Schumer, who flexed his political prowess and recruited several of the key flips last night, like former and incoming Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio to recapture the state for Democrats.

Having prevailed in a special election, Brown is expected to be seated before the end of the year.

Recent findings suggest that A Democratic staffer familiar with the current mood of the caucus predicted: “Nope. Schumer will be the leader,” when asked if there was any serious challenger.

Former Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota had a similar prediction. “Given the big night Senate Democrats had, I doubt anyone will challenge him. But some new members may withhold their vote, in keeping with their campaign comments,” Daschle noted.

Schumer on Wednesday said Democrats will be united in addressing costs for the American people with what he described as “an amazing crop of new senators” and a “generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America not only now, but on into the future.”.

Recent findings suggest that “These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want. They entrusted us with the majority to do what they, the American people, want,” he noted. “Republicans received that opportunity two years ago and completely squandered it. The GOP misread Americans’ demand for change as a mandate to do Trump’s self-serving bidding, and Trump spent half his time talking about things that were irrelevant to their lives.”.

#42795. Industry News: The Exiled Thanksgiving Dishes You Forgot Were Once on the Table

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1508 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Exiled Thanksgiving Dishes You Forgot Were Once on the Table

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was a time when Thanksgiving dinner involved gelatin—and lots of it.
  • It has been revealed that thanksgiving is a holiday that doesn’t take kindly to change.
  • Some were beloved family favorites that gradually fell out of fashion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

There was a time when Thanksgiving dinner involved gelatin—and lots of it.

It has been revealed that thanksgiving is a holiday that doesn’t take kindly to change. Suggest replacing the mashed potatoes or leaving the stuffing off the menu, and you’re likely to hear about it until Easter. Yet for all our devotion to tradition, the Thanksgiving table has changed quite a bit over the years. Somewhere along the way, entire dishes disappeared, and most of us barely noticed.

Some were beloved family favorites that gradually fell out of fashion. Others were products of an era when gelatin was considered an essential ingredient, even in dishes that had no business holding that much shape. Looking through old Thanksgiving menus, cookbooks and holiday advertisements reveals a rather wonderful assortment of foods that once had a place alongside the turkey. A few deserve to come back. Others might be better left to history, although I would very much like to meet the people responsible for them.

“Aspic” is a lovely word. It’s French, sophisticated, and just mysterious enough to suggest that whatever arrives at the table will be very impressive. You could put it on a formal dinner menu and nobody would think twice. But what you’re actually discussing is meat Jell-O.

And not some unfortunate kitchen experiment, either. Savory aspics were perfectly respectable additions to holiday meals well into the 1950s, with suspensions of meat, vegetables, seafood and even hard-boiled eggs presented in elaborate molds. The finished creations could be sliced into neat portions, allowing guests to admire every carefully arranged ingredient through a translucent wall of solidified broth.

There’s something almost admirable about the confidence required to make one of these. Imagine spending hours arranging shrimp and vegetables in a decorative mold, then carrying it proudly to the dining room as though everyone had been waiting all year for a slice of cold, wobbly meat.

Diana Chistruga for Taste of Home.

Not every gelatin creation merits as harsh a judgment as aspic. I have a certain affection for the brightly colored Jell-O salads that used to appear at holiday gatherings. There was something cheerful about a ruby-red cranberry gelatin salad or a fluffy lime concoction studded with pineapple, even if calling either one a “salad” required a fairly generous interpretation of the word.

These dishes were enormously popular in the mid-20th century, when molded gelatin desserts offered home cooks an opportunity to get creative with fruit, nuts, cream cheese, whipped topping and whatever else happened to be in the refrigerator. Some combinations were genuinely delicious. Others involved shredded carrots, celery or mayonnaise, at which point the distinction between salad and practical joke became rather difficult to maintain.

According to recent reports, I’d happily make room for a cranberry Jell-O salad at Thanksgiving. The ones made with canned tuna can remain in retirement.

Recent findings suggest that there was a time, particularly in the 1890s, when mincemeat pie was every bit as deserving of a place on the Thanksgiving dessert table as pumpkin or apple pie. Its rich filling of dried fruits, spices and citrus had a long history in English cooking, and early versions also contained actual meat—often beef or mutton—along with suet.

It has been revealed that the meat gradually disappeared from many recipes, leaving behind the sweet, deeply spiced filling that became a holiday tradition in its own right. Even so, the name has never done the pie any favors. Tell someone you’re serving mincemeat for dessert, and there’s a reasonable chance they’ll assume you’ve been sampling too many Thanksgiving cocktails.

In a recent development, that’s a shame, because a well-made mincemeat pie has plenty going for it, particularly for anyone who loves the warm flavors of cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg. It may be a harder sell than pumpkin pie, but I wouldn’t object to seeing it make a modest comeback.

Waldorf salad has much more glamorous origins than most other dishes on this list. It was created at Latest York’s Waldorf Hotel in the 1890s, originally as a simple combination of apples, celery and mayonnaise. Walnuts became a familiar addition later, and by the 1960s, the salad had found its way onto holiday tables across the country.

It has been revealed that I can understand why. The crisp apples and celery provide a welcome contrast to the rich, heavy dishes that make up Thanksgiving dinner, while the walnuts add enough substance to make it feel like more than just a bowl of chopped fruit. It’s refreshing, pleasantly crunchy and especially good alongside roasted turkey.

It has been revealed that of all the dishes that have slipped off the Thanksgiving menu, Waldorf salad might be one of the easiest to bring back. It requires very little fuss, and a fresh, crisp side is hardly unwelcome at a table already crowded with casseroles.

At some point in the ’50s, we became convinced that nearly every food could be improved by pressing it into a loaf pan.

In a recent development, the holiday vegetable loaf was one expression of that enthusiasm, turning assorted vegetables into a tidy, sliceable centerpiece with the help of binders like eggs, breadcrumbs or gelatin. Some versions were baked, while others emerged cold from the refrigerator, ready to be unmolded and presented with considerable ceremony.

In a recent development, I understand the practical appeal of preparing a dish ahead of time, particularly for Thanksgiving. What I struggle to understand is the insistence that vegetables should be made to resemble meatloaf. Carrots, peas and green beans are perfectly capable of sharing a serving dish without being pressed into a rectangular block.

Mackenzie Williams For Taste of Home.

Hot Dr Pepper sounds like something you’d find in a cookbook published during a national shortage of good judgment. But it was a genuine promotional idea, introduced by Dr Pepper in the 1960s as a way to enjoy the soft drink in colder weather.

The instructions were simple: Heat Dr Pepper, pour it into a mug and add a thin slice of lemon. The firm promoted it as a warming drink for winter gatherings, making it an intriguing candidate for the sort of holiday refreshment that now seems to have vanished almost completely.

Recent findings suggest that I can’t decide whether this is a terrible idea or one that deserves a fair trial. Dr Pepper already has a distinctive blend of sweet and spicy flavors, and warm spiced drinks are hardly unusual during the holidays. The lemon is an interesting touch, too. I wouldn’t necessarily replace the hot apple cider, but curiosity might get the better of me.

There are questionable vintage recipes, and then there are the recipes that suggest the author had finally snapped. Cranberry mayonnaise candles belong firmly in the second category.

The idea was to turn cranberry sauce and mayonnaise into a molded holiday creation resembling a candle, complete with a decorative wick or flame effect depending on the version. It was the sort of elaborate presentation that food companies once promoted with an entirely straight face, apparently confident that a candle-shaped mixture of fruit and mayonnaise was just what the Thanksgiving feast had been missing.

In a recent development, I have several questions, beginning with why the cranberry sauce needed to look like a candle and ending with why mayonnaise was invited to the party. There’s also the matter of placing something resembling a candle in the food and expecting guests to understand they’re supposed to eat it.

If you’ve ever wondered what to do with leftover turkey, the sensible answers include sandwiches, soups, potpies and perhaps casseroles. Vintage recipe developers, however, were not always interested in sensible answers.

Recent findings suggest that enter frozen jellied turkey vegetable salad, a 1970s creation that manages to combine several questionable ideas into a single dish. Turkey, vegetables and a gelatin-based mixture were assembled into a cold, molded preparation that was perhaps more ambitious than necessary.

It has been revealed that it’s difficult to imagine anyone looking at a plate of leftover turkey and deciding that what it really needed was to become a frozen, sliceable salad. Yet recipes like this reflect a period when casserole popsicles made perfect sense.

Jonathan Melendez for Taste of Home.

Industry observers note that creamed pearl onions were a familiar sight on Thanksgiving tables in the 1920s, and I think we may have been too quick to let them go. Tender little onions in a rich, buttery cream sauce are exactly the sort of thing that belongs alongside roast turkey, mashed potatoes and stuffing. They’re comforting, a little old-fashioned, and wonderfully suited to a holiday when nobody is particularly concerned about their butter intake.

They also have the advantage of feeling special without requiring an elaborate presentation. Peeling a mountain of tiny onions is admittedly nobody’s idea of holiday fun, but frozen pearl onions make the whole business much easier. If your family has never had creamed onions at Thanksgiving, this may be a tradition worth borrowing from an earlier generation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Despite the rumors I had heard about long lines and purchase limits, the new Pokemon Happy Meal was easier to get (and more adorable) than I thought.

When my son came home from summer camp a few years ago with a small pack of gifted Pokemon cards and a new hobby, I had no idea what lay ahead. Very quickly, locating Pokemon cards on shelves changed from finding them behind the register for a slightly higher price to not being able to find them at all. A renewed interest in collecting Pokemon cards has made everything Pokemon hotter than ever. And, somehow, I became a Poke-person.

Industry observers note that unwilling to pay (high) market price, my son and I have joined long lines before stores open to try and get cards. I’ve seen frenzied parents, kids and scalpers hoping to nab hard-to-find collections. One time the police were called on potential line-jumpers. So, when I heard McDonald’s Pokemon Happy Meals were coming, I had no idea if I’d be able to purchase one or if they were going to sell out immediately. I’m too deep into the world of Pokemon not to try, and what shocked me the most was how simple it was!

Melissa Gaman For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, A McDonald’s Pokemon Happy Meal is a regular Happy Meal housed in one of three Pokemon-themed boxes, though sadly ours was in a regular red box. Each meal has a small box with one of 15 Pokemon toys and two cards. There are 15 cards in this promotion, and seven of them have shiny foil holographic elements. Each toy features a Pokemon character in the shape of a mini Happy Meal. It has a hinged plastic clip on the back so you can attach it to a bag or flip it up and use it as a card holder. The meal also had unexpectedly fun pouches of Pokemon-designed apple slices.

Some websites claimed that during the five-week promotion, there would be specific Pokemon toys allotted for each week, but if that was the plan, it’s already off track. We received two Pokemon that were supposedly marked for week three, and various Poke-loving social media posts showed off photos with an assortment of all 15 characters.

Melissa Gaman For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, before the launch, there was speculation that Pokemon Happy Meals would be limited to one per customer or potentially sold only if a child was present, in an effort to fight scalpers. I couldn’t find anything official from McDonald’s or Pokemon Center on this policy, and it wasn’t my experience. When I ordered with my son, we asked for two, and there was no mention of limits. The solo woman behind me ordered without glitch.

It has been revealed that the line at my local McDonald’s was long, but mostly because we headed there right after school, when plenty of hungry teenagers were there. I saw only a few other people opening Pokemon toys, so for all the buzz around this collab, it was my easiest Pokemon experience in years.

Pokemon Happy Meals will be available in the U.S. until Dec. 14. However, the most notable thing to remember is that this promotion is while supplies last. Considering that reseller sites like eBay are already buzzing with toys and cards, there is a good chance supplies will sell out before then.

Even though our fries were cold, the toys are adorable, and the art on the cards is Poke-perfection. I don’t think we will catch them all, but hopefully we can get a few more while they are available.

In a recent development, will you be trying to collect one or all of the toys and cards? Let us know in the comments!

  • It has been revealed that for Chavarria and Lopez, whose respective designs draw on Chicano and Dominican-American cultural references, these conversations have long been part of their work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, willy Chavarria and Raul Lopez of LUAR are among the designers participating in Malvestir, a major newly introduced exhibition at MoMA PS1 examining the relationship between Latin American fashion and contemporary art announced today. Opening April 22, 2027, the exhibition will feature work by 20 artists and designers from across the Americas, bringing together clothing, photography, sculpture, and textiles to explore how dress reflects questions of cultural identity, class, and power.

It has been revealed that for Chavarria and Lopez, whose respective designs draw on Chicano and Dominican-American cultural references, these conversations have long been part of their work. Both have built internationally recognized labels that incorporate the aesthetics and experiences of communities historically underrepresented within luxury fashion.

Industry observers note that “Being part of this exhibition at MoMA PS1 is deeply meaningful to me. It’s an opportunity to share a piece of who I am, where I come from, and the culture that has shaped me. I’m proud to be part of a moment that gives space to Latino voices and celebrates the beauty, creativity, and richness of our culture,” Chavarria tells Vogue.

It has been revealed that josh Tafoya. Bad Hombre. 2026. Hand woven Serape style cape in Churro wool. Multi panels with Rio grande, Chimayo, and Vallero styles. Hand sewn with natural dyed wool warp. With spotted black and white hair on hide chaps. Hand cut fringe. Courtesy the artist.

Recent findings suggest that lopez, meanwhile, has built LUAR around his experiences growing up in New York, drawing on Dominican culture, queer nightlife, and the city’s amorphous approach to getting dressed. “I grew up in New York in a Dominican family, around people who could make a whole look out of whatever they had. The fashion industry has always pulled from communities like mine. With LUAR, I’ve always wanted us to be the ones telling those stories. Being part of Malvestir at MoMA PS1 feels personal because I get to bring that point of view into the room alongside artists and designers with their own stories about what it means to get dressed across Latin America and the diaspora,” Lopez tells Vogue.

Sources indicate that the exhibition’s title offers some insight into its broader themes. A combination of the Spanish words mal (“poorly”) and vestir (“to dress”), Malvestir references the colonial-era designation malvestidos, applied to those whose clothing did not conform to prescribed boundaries of race, caste, or gender. The term remains pejorative, but can also express a rejection of established conventions of taste and social class. The exhibition considers these histories alongside the ways artists and designers use clothing to express identity today.

Leonardo Choxom. Performance, from the series Piezas Experimentales, 2023-2024. Textile. Courtesy the artist. © Leonardo Choxom.

Industry observers note that josé Ballivian. La virgen viste de Balenciaga. 2024. Pencil on paper. 100 x 70 cm. Courtesy the artist.

In a recent development, organized by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will bring together artists working across a wide range of disciplines. Colombian photographer Camila Falquez’s ongoing series Syncretism, for example, features portraits of queer and trans people from Latin America and the Caribbean, drawing on Indigenous and African spiritual traditions. Mexican designer Carla Fernández, known for her collaborations with Indigenous artisans, will also participate, alongside Bolivian artist José Ballivián, whose drawings place familiar luxury and sportswear logos within traditional Andean imagery.

Industry observers note that other works address the global movement of clothing and its environmental and economic consequences. Guatemalan artist David Ramírez Cotón draws on his family’s experience running a secondhand clothing business in Guatemala City, while Venezuelan artist Cassandra Mayela uses garments collected from Venezuelan migrants in her large-scale woven works. The Afro-Colombian collective Las Tejedoras de Mampuján will contribute a newly commissioned tapestry depicting the reuse and recycling of textiles within its workshop. The influence of Western luxury and beauty advertising also comes under examination: Costa Rican artist La Cholla Jackson, for instance, reimagines a Dior campaign from the 2000s, posing with accessories constructed from discarded materials.

Barbara Sánchez-Kane. Lessons in Draping. 2023, rawhide, metal, wood. 325 × 92 × 84 cm. Image courtesy of the artist and kurimanzutto Mexico City / Newly introduced York. © Bárbara Sánchez-Kane. Photo: Da Brandica.

Patrica Belli. Mamá (detail). 2021. Clothing, rope, buckles. 194 x 335 x 172 cm. Courtesy of the artist and Parallel Oaxaca.

“Malvestir reimagines how fashion can be displayed in museums, reflecting the very alive possibilities and contradictions inherent to the form. The show offers a provocative, materially rich look at 20 artists and designers across the Americas who are in dialogue with one another, yet have never been brought together in an exhibition until now,” Ketelsen González tells Vogue.

It has been revealed that malvestir arrives amid a wider cultural interest in fashion as a means of exploring identity, heritage, and power. Following the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s 2025 exhibition Superfine: Tailoring Black Style, which examined the history of Black dandyism and its relationship to identity across the Atlantic diaspora, the MoMA PS1 show continues a broader conversation about the cultural and political significance of dress. It also builds on MoMA PS1’s own history of presenting fashion alongside contemporary art, dating back to its experimental fashion programming in the early 1980s.

According to recent reports, installation View: Se abrió paca, David Ramírez Cotón. All pieces acrylic on canvas, variable measurements, 2024. Curated by Josseline Pinto at La Galería Rebelde, Guatemala City. Photo: courtesy of La Galería Rebelde.

Recent findings suggest that willy Chavarria. Safe from Harm (still) 2024. Courtesy the artist and MATTE. © Willy Chavarria.

It has been revealed that “Malvestir addresses urgent, shared concerns across fashion, contemporary art, and visual culture, engaging daring artists and designers both in Upcoming York and across the Americas. MoMA PS1 has a history of presenting innovative designers alongside contemporary artists. We’re thrilled that audiences will be able to experience the formal experimentation, political imagination, and cultural contradictions at the heart of Malvestir,” says Butler.

Malvestir will be on view at MoMA PS1 from April 22 through September 6, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Recent findings suggest that cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Sources indicate that remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

How redrawn House districts voted in the midterms

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Texas Democrat Johnny Garcia, here speaking to campaign volunteers in San Antonio in September, won a district that state Republicans redrew to favor their party.
  • In a recent development, house Republicans were banking on their redistricting power play as a firewall against Democratic gains.
  • It has been revealed that redraws of congressional maps across the country reshaped the fight for the House, putting new districts on the battleground and setting up some surprisingly close races.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Texas Democrat Johnny Garcia, here speaking to campaign volunteers in San Antonio in September, won a district that state Republicans redrew to favor their party. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, house Republicans were banking on their redistricting power play as a firewall against Democratic gains. But a blue “tsunami” tore right through it.

It has been revealed that redraws of congressional maps across the country reshaped the fight for the House, putting new districts on the battleground and setting up some surprisingly close races. But Democrats ended up losing only a few gerrymandered seats, and none held by a Democratic incumbent seeking reelection.

According to recent reports, in North Carolina, where Republicans redrew the map this cycle, Democrats had flipped five GOP-held seats through Nov. 10, all of which had been considered safe or on the periphery of the House battleground.

In a recent development, “We made it clear last year … that Republicans might start this redistricting and gerrymandering. Democrats were going to finish it. And last night that’s exactly what happened,” Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat, said at a news conference on Nov. 4.

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump kicked off the redistricting effort last summer, when he called for Texas to redraw its congressional lines. Democrats responded in California, where voters approved a upcoming map that would give the party five pickup opportunities.

According to recent reports, in total, nine states held elections in 2026 under latest House maps, and attempts to redraw the congressional lines in other states fell short. Virginia Democrats were dealt a setback when the commonwealth’s Supreme Court invalidated a Democrat-led redraw that voters had approved via a referendum. Similarly, the U.S. Supreme Court blocked Republicans from using a redrawn map in Missouri, which voters rejected via a referendum on Election Day.

Efforts to adopt newly introduced maps in Republican-led Indiana, South Carolina and Georgia also came up short.

Here’s how candidates running in redrawn districts fared on election night:.

Democrats held four of the five seats that Texas Republicans targeted through redistricting.

32nd District: Republican Air Force veteran Jace Yarbrough narrowly defeated Democrat Dan Barrios, a former Richardson City Council member, in a redrawn district that would have backed the president by 18 points in 2024.

9th District: The Houston-area district would have backed Trump by 20 points under the new lines, but Democrat Leticia Gutierrez comfortably held the seat for her party over Republican Army veteran Alex Mealer.

35th District: Democrat Johnny Garcia, a former Bexar County sheriff’s deputy, defeated Republican Air Force veteran Carlos De La Cruz in a redrawn San Antonio-area district that Trump would have carried by 10 points.

28th District: Longtime Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar’s South Texas seat was another Republican target, but he defeated party-switching Webb County Judge Tano Tijerina in a landslide.

34th District: Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez coasted to reelection over Republican Eric Flores, a former federal prosecutor, in a redrawn Trump +10 South Texas district.

Texas Democrats also flipped the massive 23rd District, which hugs the U.S.-Mexico border, and the 15th District in South Texas.

Florida Republicans were hoping to pick up as many as four seats under their new map, but Democrats have held on to all of them.

Industry observers note that 9th District: Rep. Darren Soto, who went into Election Day as the most vulnerable House Democrat, defeated Republican Navy veteran Dan Green in a redrawn Central Florida seat that Trump would have carried it by 18 points.

14th District: Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor held off a challenge from Republican former state Rep. Mike Beltran, despite her Tampa Bay district transforming into one that would have backed Trump by 11 points.

22nd District: Democrat Pia Dandiya kept this open South Florida seat in party hands, defeating Republican Casey Askar in a Trump +10 district.

25th District: Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz defeated Republican former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer in a Trump +9 district that hosted one of the most expensive House races this year.

Ohio was required under state law to draw a new map ahead of the 2026 elections. In a surprise, Republicans and Democrats on the state’s redistricting commission struck a deal that resulted in new lines that favored the GOP, but not as much as Democrats had feared.

In a recent development, 9th District: Rep. Marcy Kaptur, the longest-serving woman in congressional history, won her rematch against Republican former state Rep. Derek Merrin by an even wider margin in a Toledo-area district that would have backed Trump by 11 points.

1st District: Rep. Greg Landsman had no trouble winning reelection over Republican Eric Conroy, a former Air Force intelligence officer, in a redrawn Trump +3 district in the Cincinnati area.

In addition, Ohio Democrats knocked off GOP incumbents in the 7th, 10th and 15th districts.

It wasn’t a surprise that North Carolina joined the GOP-led redistricting push; the latest 2026 map was the state’s sixth in seven election cycles and gave Republicans the edge in 11 out of 14 seats. The primary focus of the new GOP-drawn map was the 1st District, but as of Nov. 10, four Republican incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chair Richard Hudson, had lost their bids and a fifth was trailing.

1st District: Rep. Don Davis’ Eastern North Carolina seat grew more competitive under the fresh map, shifting to one Trump would have carried by 12 points. But the second-term Democrat won his rematch over Republican Army veteran Laurie Buckhout.

In a recent development, after the Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais ruling that weakened parts of the Voting Rights Act , the court allowed Alabama to use a latest map that would favor Republicans in a district that had been drawn the previous cycle as a second Black-opportunity district.

According to recent reports, 2nd District: This plurality-Black, Kamala Harris-voting district was redrawn as one Trump would have carried by 14 points. Nevertheless, Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures comfortably prevailed over Republican state Rep. Rhett Marques.

After the Supreme Court invalidated Louisiana’s congressional map under the Callais ruling, state Republicans adopted latest boundaries expected to help them flip one seat.

6th District: The latest map eliminated the majority-Black seat created the previous cycle, which the Supreme Court ruled was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander. Democratic Rep. Cleo Fields opted to run for the state Senate instead of seeking reelection in a redrawn Trump +32 district. This year’s election reverted to Louisiana’s “jungle” primary system, with all candidates running on the same ballot. And with no one likely to take a majority of the primary vote, the top two finishers will advance to a Dec. 12 runoff.

Tennessee Republicans moved promptly after the Callais ruling, adopting a map that gave them the advantage in all nine of the state’s House seats.

It has been revealed that 9th District: The Memphis-based district, a formerly deep-blue bastion, was dramatically redrawn as a seat Trump would have carried by 21 points. And yet Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor eked out a victory over Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson.

Recent findings suggest that california’s new voter-approved map led to significant reshuffling in the state delegation, setting up a member-versus-member fight and prompting Republican Rep. Kevin Kiley to become an independent.

Recent findings suggest that 1st District: Republican James Gallagher, who topped CQ Roll Call’s final list of the most vulnerable House members, lost to Democratic former state Senate leader Mike McGuire in a Harris +12 Northern California district. Gallagher won a June special election under the old lines to succeed the late GOP Rep. Doug LaMalfa.

3rd District: The latest map redrew Kiley’s 3rd District as a solid-blue Sacramento-area seat, prompting Democratic Rep. Ami Bera to seek reelection here. Kiley opted for the slightly-less-blue 6th District but was defeated by former Democratic state Sen. Richard Pan.

22nd District: GOP Rep. David Valadao saw his purple Central Valley seat moved a tad left, though Trump would still have carried it. Still, the Republican lost to progressive Democrat Randy Villegas.

41st District: Redistricting dismantled Rep. Ken Calvert’s Riverside County seat, and he opted to challenge fellow GOP Rep. Young Kim in the deep-red 40th District. Democratic Rep. Linda T. Sánchez won the newly introduced 41st, now a blue stronghold in Los Angeles County.

48th District: Republican Rep. Darrell Issa announced his retirement after the upcoming map transformed his deep-red Southern California seat into a purple battleground. Democrat Marni von Wilpert, a San Diego city councilmember, defeated Republican Jim Desmond, a San Diego county supervisor.

In a recent development, A Utah judge approved a new map that gave Democrats a pickup opportunity and set off a round of musical chairs among the state’s four Republican House members that culminated with Rep. Burgess Owens opting to retire.

#42785. The Best Cast-Iron Skillets for a Lifetime of Cooking (2026)
