The Best Cast-Iron Skillets for a Lifetime of Cooking (2026)

📅 16 Jun 2021 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet.
  • There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.
  • To these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet. There is a die-hard fan base loyal to the affordable US-made Lodge cast-iron pan that will not hear of any other suggestions.

There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

To these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”.

If you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t; either way, I’m happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

According to recent reports, cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be said for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

It has been revealed that yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think, and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

And cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a burnished crispy exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast iron alongside its stainless-steel and carbon steel pans and enameled Dutch oven.

New in this update: A review of Made In's new cast-iron pan as well as more long-term testing information for our winner.

Size(s): 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

Recent findings suggest that what I loved: Because they’re much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the new era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small manufacturer based in Southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

The Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 lb. for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 lb. or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly significant difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

Sources indicate that it has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron, though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes pre-seasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties, though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

Other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

An earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

What I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I’ll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

It has been revealed that in the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn’t that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I’ve found that this doesn’t impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

Below you’ll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn’t have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some gray patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won’t hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don’t let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you’re really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff off the excess, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

Industry observers note that some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it’s a record of use and proof that it’s growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you’re just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

If you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

Size(s): 4.8" (1.1 lb.), 6.5" (2 lb.), 8" (3.1 lb.), 10" (5.5 lb.), 12" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

What I loved: Again, I apologize for snubbing Lodge, as even in our office we have a number of staunch brand loyalists. But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are pre-seasoned with flaxseed oil and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough pre-seasoning is more crucial on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. But we know that some people want as much of a head start as they can get, and this pan offers you the best one.

According to recent reports, the other way the Victoria bested the Lodge is in its form factor. The pour spouts on the Victoria are nice and wide, making it easy to pour off oil or other pan juices, and testers found the handle shape slightly more comfortable than the Lodge.

I’ll be honest, though, these differences are pretty small, and if you feel drawn to the Lodge name, I recommend it as well.

It has been revealed that what I’d leave: Given it’s bargain pricing, there isn’t much to dislike here. I will note this pan is significantly heavier than the Lancaster pan—a full pound and a half for the same diameter skillet. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it’s a trade-off you’ll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

Industry observers note that 1. We had several members of staff handle the pans to get a broad sense of how easy the pans were to maneuver. Then we got to cooking.

2. Using a little bit of oil, we fried eggs sunny-side up and scrambled to see how much (if anything) stuck to the pan.

In a recent development, 3. We seared skin-on chicken thighs to get a sense of how evenly heat was distributed around the cooking surface. We also measured how long it took for the pan to reach 375° at medium heat.

According to recent reports, 4. We washed the pans in hot water, noting any places where seasoning might have worn away.

Sources indicate that 5. We re-seasoned the pans ourselves in an oven for an hour at 500°.

Sources indicate that 6. We cooked another round of eggs to observe any changes.

In a recent development, I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

Sizing is a bit different from tech giant to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

How nonstick is the pan out of the box?

I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we’re talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

Heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon steel frying pans get hot swiftly, but they don’t always have the heat-retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear safely with them.

Stargazer Cast Iron Skillet - 10.5".

The Stargazer is a lovely pan. Like the Lancaster, its a vintage-style skillet, so it has a smooth texture that’s easy to clean. The surface develops seasoning well, and the curved lip allows for easy pouring at any angle. Ultimately, it is one of the heavier high-end skillets available on the market, which is why we don’t have it as a winner. However, if weight isn’t a huge concern for you, it is still an excellent pan.

If you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a new name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. This pan has a nice velvety surface that holds on to seasoning very well, while still maintaining a smooth, glossier finish that makes vintage-style pans so desirable. Small gripes: The handle design wasn’t a favorite among testers, and the side walls are a slightly shorter than most other cast-iron pans. It’s also a touch heavier and a couple touches more expensive than our winner. Still, this is an excellent cast-iron pan and makes a great family heirloom.

Lodge Cast-Iron Skillet with Red Mini Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 8".

In a recent development, people who track recommendations like these tend to be shocked that we don’t place the Lodge as our winner or budget pick. It is a fantastic pan, make no mistake. It has a great factory seasoning that’s resilient from the jump, and the 10" costs around twenty bucks—so what gives? When it came down to it, the Victoria pan had a slicker factory seasoning out of the box and a more comfortable handle design.

Smithey No. 10 Cast-Iron Skillet.

Industry observers note that another high-end polished cast-iron pan on the list. Smithey pans are gorgeous, so much so that it almost feels wrong cooking with them. However, you should cook with it straight away, as the factory seasoning is a little light on these, and we observed a little bit wearing away after the first couple rounds of cooking prior to us adding an additional layer of seasoning. Senior editor Noah Kaufman has been cooking with the Smithey multiple times a week for a couple years and notes that within a few months of regular use and two bouts of seasoning in the oven he no longer worried about stuck eggs or steaks.

Gorgeous as they are, Smithey pans are heavy, though, at 5.8 lb. for the 10" skillet.

In a recent development, this skillet is the second lightest (4.3 lb. at 10") and has a velvety surface that holds on to seasoning a little better than the smooth polished pans. Like the Stargazer, it also has a curved lip instead of a pour spout, but I found that this pan does have a bit of a dribbling problem, which I wasn't crazy about. Still, one member of our team who has now lived with this pan for years loves it and uses it every day.

Lodge Cast-Iron Blacklock Skillet, Triple Seasoned - 10.25".

Lodge released this pan in response to the wave of newly introduced and fancy polished pans, and as beautiful (quite beautiful), well-seasoned (three glossy layers), and lightweight as it is (almost even with the Lancaster), our testers found the handle uncomfortable to hold.

Ooni is a pizza oven organization, and this pan is really designed for cooking in an oven rather than on the stovetop. It has a detachable handle, which is actually a genius bit of design that makes it easy and comfortable to grab out of a blazing hot pizza oven. But the sides are too shallow for doing more normal cast-iron things like frying chicken or sautéing greens. It is, however, great for cornbread and pizookies.

Recent findings suggest that this is Made In’s official entry into the cast-iron new wave. The pan has a smooth machined surface, nice design touches, like curved sidewalls and a spacious helper handle. The primary handle is nice to hold; however, a longer handle can make a pan feel heavier and add strain on the wrists. This pan is not the lightest, either. I found it difficult to transport the full pan from the stovetop to the oven using only one hand, so consider this a pan for people with meaty forearms. Made In also uses flaxseed oil for the factory seasoning, which is a controversial choice in the cast-iron world. The reason for that controversy is that, while the finish flaxseed oil produces is glossy and attractive, it tends to be brittle. Especially with newer pans, a flaxseed seasoning has a tendency to wear away with regular cooking. After testing, I did notice this pan had some gray (unseasoned) patches after a round of searing meat. Again, not a major deal—just keep cooking with it— but something to keep in mind. All of that being noted, I do still think this is a high-quality pan. During the cooking tests, I had absolutely no issues with sticking whatsoever.

This pan is pretty similar to a standard Lodge or Victoria, but with a seasoning that’s not as nonstick out of the box. We did find, however, that it added new layers of seasoning quite well.

Valor Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Skillet.

Recent findings suggest that the Valor is apparently a favorite in restaurants, but there’s nothing special to it that makes it stand out. If anything, the pour spouts are so small they might as well not be there at all.

According to recent reports, we’re all for innovation, which is what Finex sought to do with its octagonal pan and its bulbous handle, but we didn’t really observe any value from the modifications. While the octagonal shape is easier for flipping you could just use a bigger cast-iron pan for anything you want to flip. And its “speed cool” handle was awkward to hold.

Industry observers note that anytime KitchenAid ventures beyond the small appliance space you never quite know what you’re gonna get. In this case, it’s a cast-iron pan that is totally average in every way, except for its minimalist modern design. We think this pan is too expensive for what you’re getting.

Industry observers note that “Ooh, a lid!” Was the universal reaction to this cast-iron pan. If you like the idea of having a lid for your pan, then this is your pan. The problem with cast-iron lids, though, is that they don’t benefit from the progressive seasoning development the rest of the pan gets as you cook with it. Lids are only really dealing with evaporative moisture, which makes them even more likely to rust. Smithey, up above, sells glass lids that fit their pans, which, while not as oven-safe, won’t have that rust problem.

Recent findings suggest that this is Victoria’s answer to the high-end polished cast-iron pan. The seasoning is great, but the pan is heavier than the Lancaster, and we didn’t love all the extra design embellishments. The brass insert on the handle had no practical value (it heated up quicker than the surrounding cast iron). Also, all the extra ridges and divots just meant more places for gunk to get stuck in.

Amazon customers really like this pan. It comes with a silicone handle cover and a glass lid, which is nice (glass is a better material for a lid than cast iron). It also has tall 3" sides that make this pan great for frying. Beyond that, though, the pan is heavy and seemed to be barely pre-seasoned.

This is a super polished cast-iron pan with a glossy cooking surface that was nice to work with. However, we noticed quite a few cosmetic issues, like small nicks and rough edges that made it seem like there were some corners cut in the manufacturing process.

It has been revealed that another pan that is just fine. The factory seasoning is minimal, so you’ll have to build that up yourself. There are several better options that are just as affordable from Victoria, Lodge, and others.

This is an affordable pan that looks a lot like a Lodge, but with a lesser factory seasoning.

Amazon Basics Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Pan.

The seasoning that came on this pan out of the box was pretty bad, and with so many other cheap alternatives that offer much better quality, we don’t see the point in purchasing this pan. It’s also only available in a 15" diameter at the time of writing, which is bigger (and heavier) than most people need.

It has been revealed that when you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as pre-seasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

No, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.).

For really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Recent findings suggest that tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.).

If, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

Sources indicate that wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit’s resident cookware tester and researcher for over six years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a big apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 matter of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

It has been revealed that whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Industry observers note that absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

In a recent development, IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

It has been revealed that IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wendy’s is getting nostalgic this holiday season, and as someone who grew up eating in one of the chain’s iconic glass sunrooms, I’m particularly excited about this one.

The fast food chain just introduced a limited-time Holiday Box complete with retro packaging, collectible knit hats, and a choice of some familiar menu favorites. And of course, two new peppermint-inspired Frosty desserts.

Obviously, I had to try everything for myself.

Available beginning November 16 at participating Wendy’s locations nationwide, the Holiday Box starts at $11.99 and includes your choice of a Dave’s Double or 10-piece crispy or spicy chicken nuggets, small fries, a small soft drink, and one collectible knit hat.

The packaging is designed to resemble Wendy’s old-school Solarium restaurants, complete with the recognizable glass-walled dining area that became a staple of the chain beginning in the 1980s.

And I have to admit, this one hit me right in the childhood memories.

It has been revealed that growing up, I remember going to Wendy’s with my mom and sitting in that yellow, glass-enclosed sunroom. Seeing the design recreated as a miniature holiday box immediately brought me back to those visits.

Each Holiday Box includes one of four collectible knit hats featuring a retro Wendy’s design: Frosty, Biggie, the classic Wendy’s logo, or the famous “Where’s the Beef?” slogan.

The hats come in sealed mystery bags, meaning you won’t know which one you’re getting until you open it.

Thankfully, I ended up with the blue Frosty beanie, which was exactly the design I was hoping for.

Had I opened the bag to find a hat with “Biggie” written across my forehead, though, I think we would’ve had a problem.

The Holiday Box is available for a limited time while supplies last, and customers can’t select which hat they receive.

Alongside the Holiday Box, Wendy’s is introducing two limited-time desserts: the Peppermint Frosty Swirl and Peppermint Brownie Frosty Fusion.

Both are available with either a vanilla or chocolate Frosty base, so I decided to try one of each.

This was easily my favorite of the two.

The Peppermint Brownie Frosty Fusion combines Wendy’s classic Frosty with peppermint sauce and brownie pieces, creating a dessert that feels especially appropriate for the holiday season.

I went with the vanilla base, and I absolutely loved it.

Sources indicate that the peppermint flavor was strong and immediately reminded me of a candy cane or a York Peppermint Pattie. It had that recognizable minty sweetness I look for in a holiday dessert, without getting lost in the vanilla Frosty.

The brownie pieces were another highlight, adding a nice texture and a layer of chocolate flavor to the mix. I particularly liked how the chocolate complemented the peppermint rather than competing with it.

In a recent development, for me, this is exactly what a seasonal Frosty should taste like. It’s festive, flavorful, and different enough from the regular menu to make it worth trying.

For my second dessert, I went with the chocolate Peppermint Frosty Swirl, which combines Wendy’s classic Chocolate Frosty with peppermint sauce.

My biggest piece of advice is to give this one a good stir before digging in.

Sources indicate that when I first tried it, most of the peppermint syrup was concentrated toward the top of the dessert. Mixing everything together helped distribute the flavor more evenly throughout the Frosty.

Once I did that, I really enjoyed it.

The combination of chocolate and peppermint works well, although I didn’t find the mint flavor nearly as strong as it was in the vanilla Brownie Frosty Fusion.

Industry observers note that still, I’m happy to report that Wendy’s peppermint sauce works with both Frosty flavors. If you prefer a more straightforward chocolate-mint combination without brownie pieces, this is a solid option.

Personally, though, I’d go back for the Fusion.

People across the country take breakfast very seriously—after all, many believe it's the most important meal of the day. When you're rushing to work, grabbing something on the go is often the easiest option. And nothing screams breakfast quite like a side of hash browns. When a diner isn't in the cards, a fast food chain can be just the ticket.

According to recent reports, I tried hash browns from five different fast food chains to see which one serves up the best during the morning rush. Of the chains I tried, only Dunkin' serves hash browns all day. Everywhere else, you'll need to order during breakfast hours, which vary by location.

This proved to be one of the tougher taste tests I've conducted during my time at Delish. There were truly no terrible options, and some of the differences were pretty small. Here's how they stacked up.

Burger King's hash browns come in a handy carton filled with plenty of small, round crisps. They have a crunchy exterior and, honestly, are perfectly adequate. They're just up against some tough contenders. Of all the spuds I tried, these were the least memorable and had the least flavor, though nothing about them was off-putting.

Industry observers note that taco Bell served the most substantial hash brown on this list—it was quite hefty. The exterior had a nice crispiness, but compared to its competitors, the inside was much mushier, and the whole thing was noticeably greasier. It's not something I could eat a lot of.

In a recent development, dunkin's hash browns, which are served all day (!), were a bit more divisive in the Delish office. Some people stood ten toes down for the zesty onion flavor, while others (myself included) found it more reminiscent of leftover grease on a stove. That said, the texture was great, and whether you love them or hate them, these had the boldest flavor and stood out from the rest of the pack.

Industry observers note that like Taco Bell, McDonald's offers a larger hash brown patty than the others on this list. The chain totally nails the crispy outer edges and boasts great potato flavor. You can really tell this is McDonald's because the taste is so similar to the chain's iconic fries. If you like those, you'll love its hash browns. However, because of the patty's size, the middle lost some of the structure and crispiness I was looking for.

In a surprise win, Chick-fil-A's hash browns came out on top. The bite-sized pieces are easy to grab on the go, and their small size gives each one the perfect mix of a crispy exterior and soft interior. The flavor is spot-on, with savory onion and pepper notes. Best of all, they weren't overly greasy.

Industry observers note that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

According to recent reports, these maple-glazed carrots don’t hold back on the butter—or the brown sugar. Roasted with pure maple syrup and crushed red pepper flakes, they turn tender and glossy with a sweet-hot kick that complements everything from ham to lamb to green bean casserole.

The recipe began with Barbie—not the doll, but Andy Baraghani’s cousin’s former girlfriend. Her syrupy-sweet carrots became a fixture at family Christmas dinners. Some dishes are meant to last; some relationships aren’t.

According to recent reports, for BA’s version, Andy traded the original’s hours-long cooking time for a hotter roast that gives the carrots browned edges and a buttery glaze. There’s no separate sauce to simmer: Everything goes straight onto a foil-lined (for easier cleanup) rimmed baking sheet, with regular tossing to coat the carrots in syrup as they cook. No. This recipe calls for scrubbed, unpeeled carrots—give them a thorough cleaning and leave the skins on.

How do I keep the glaze from burning?

It has been revealed that keep the carrot pieces similar in thickness, halving or quartering larger ones lengthwise. Check the glaze each time you toss the carrots, especially once the edges begin browning: The sugars can darken promptly. Use tenderness and browned edges as your guide rather than waiting out the clock if the carrots are already done.

For a more savory version, try our Easy Roasted Carrots.

Place rack in middle of oven and preheat oven to 400°. Line a rimmed baking sheet with 3 sheets of foil (you’ll need it!). Cut 2 lb. medium carrots, tops trimmed to about ½", scrubbed, on a diagonal into 3" pieces (halved or quartered lengthwise if large).

Spread out carrots on foil. Evenly top with 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, ⅓ cup (packed; 70 g) light brown sugar, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Season with kosher salt and toss to combine.

Sources indicate that roast carrots, tossing every 20 minutes, until tender and browned around the edges, 50–60 minutes. Watch closely as the carrots begin to brown; the glaze can darken swiftly. Transfer to a platter and drizzle with any remaining syrup. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt (if using).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the future of 84 KFC and KFC/Taco Bell restaurants across 10 states is uncertain after one of the chain’s franchisees filed for bankruptcy. The operator, Tasty Chick’n, filed for Chapter 11 protection in Texas on November 16.

The company entered into franchise agreements in 2021 with KFC and Taco Bell, both owned by Yum! Brands. Tasty Chick’n’s portfolio includes 75 KFC restaurants and nine co-branded locations across Tennessee, Florida, Virginia, Arkansas, Kentucky, Illinois, Missouri, Alabama, Mississippi, and Indiana.

In its bankruptcy filing, Tasty Chick’n notes that sales have declined by 15.6 percent over the past three fiscal years while operating costs have skyrocketed. So far in 2026, restaurant-level profit margins have dropped to just 4 percent, down from 11 percent in 2023. And under its franchise agreements, nearly half of the franchisees’ locations require substantial and expensive upgrades through 2029.

According to recent reports, tasty Chick’n began deferring royalty payments in mid-2025 and generally stopped paying them altogether that November. This past September, KFC and Taco Bell’s franchising entities issued a notice of intent to terminate their agreements, claiming the operator owed nearly $16 million in unpaid royalties and other fees. Tasty Chick’n also faces approximately 14 lawsuits from landlords in five states over unpaid rent and other charges. The bankruptcy filing revealed that the operator has accrued nearly $73 million in funded debt.

Industry observers note that the fate of the restaurants remains undecided. Tasty Chick’n is planning a court-supervised sale of its portfolio, either in its entirety or divided into different regional markets. Whether buyers will bite is another story, especially given KFC’s overall trajectory. A report earlier this year revealed that KFC had shuttered more than 300 locations between July 2025 and July 2026 alone.

No matter what happens to these KFC locations, this bankruptcy is another reminder of just how tough 2026 has been for fast food operators.

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

According to recent reports, cranberry crackle salad combines crunchy and creamy textures with sweet and tangy flavors. It's a retro-style dessert with a hearty dose of seasonal cheer.

I live in cranberry country (aka northern Wisconsin), and when fresh cranberries hit store shelves, there’s a good chance you’ll find me in the kitchen baking with them. One sweet treat that often finds its way onto our holiday brunch menus is a loaf (or three) of cranberry-orange bread. There’s just something so cozy about the combination of tart cranberries and sweet, bright orange juice—the inspiration for this cranberry crackle salad recipe.

Recent findings suggest that crackle salad is a variation on retro fluff salad that combines cream cheese, whipped topping and fruit mix-ins with a crunchy, candied “crackle” topping (made with crushed pretzels, chopped pecans, brown sugar and melted butter). In this holiday-inspired crackle salad, the cream mixture is flavored with whole-berry cranberry sauce and orange zest. Fresh orange juice in the crackle adds a subtle citrus flavor, too. This recipe makes enough for a small crowd, and is perfect for sharing at a Thanksgiving potluck or as a fun throwback side dish at holiday gatherings.

According to recent reports, preheat the oven to 400°F. Line a 15x10x1-inch rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat.

In a large bowl, stir together the broken pretzels, chopped pecans and brown sugar. Stir in the melted butter and orange juice to coat.

Spread the pretzel mixture in an even layer on the prepared baking sheet. Bake it for five to eight minutes or until it’s bubbly. Let it cool completely on the baking sheet before breaking it into pieces.

Editor’s Tip: Keep your eye on the crackle as it bakes; it can easily burn if baked too long.

Recent findings suggest that in a large bowl, beat together the softened cream cheese and vanilla. Stir in the cranberry sauce until it’s combined. Gently fold in the whipped topping until it’s incorporated.

Sources indicate that fold in the orange zest. Cover the bowl and refrigerate the mixture for at least one hour.

Recent findings suggest that just before serving, stir in half of the pretzel mixture. Top the salad with the remaining pretzel mixture to serve. If you like, add sugared cranberries as an additional garnish.

Editor’s Tip: Avoid adding the crunch to the salad too early, as it will soften up over time.

Industry observers note that leftover cranberry crackle salad should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge. It will last for up to three days in the fridge. The crackle will soften over time once added to the salad.

In a recent development, any extra crackle topping should be stored in an airtight container at room temperature to keep it crunchy. It should keep for up to one week.

It has been revealed that you can make the cream mixture and crackle up to two day in advance. Store the salad and crackle separately, and don’t combine them until just before serving the salad.

If you want to dial up the crunch factor even more, allow the baked crackle to cool thoroughly before using it. This will ensure it has the crunchiest texture.

Fresh cranberries are a great option when they are in season. To make this cranberry crackle salad with fresh cranberries, you’ll need a 12-ounce package of whole cranberries. (You could also use frozen whole cranberries, but they need to thaw first.).

According to recent reports, in a food processor or blender, pulse the berries until they’re finely chopped. Pour the berries into a large bowl and stir in 1/2 cup of granulated sugar. Cover and refrigerate them for at least one hour or overnight. Use the fresh berry mixture in place of the canned cranberry sauce in this recipe.

This cranberry crackle salad will fit right in with any holiday potluck spread. It’s also a fun retro dessert salad to share at a holiday meal alongside classic savory offerings such as roasted turkey, mashed potatoes and green bean casserole.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Reflecting on Tuesday’s midterm election results, a shellacking by Democrats that served as a rebuke to President Donald Trump, this quote deserves another look.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., talks with reporters in the basement of the Capitol on June 21, 2016. Back then, the late senator had a different view of President Donald Trump, Curtis writes. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

“If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed ... and we will deserve it.”.

Reflecting on Tuesday’s midterm election results, a shellacking by Democrats that served as a rebuke to President Donald Trump, this quote deserves another look.

Sources indicate that in 2016, in the midst of a heated Republican primary race, with assorted candidates jockeying to be the party’s presidential nominee, those words were posted by what now seems a surprising source: South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Industry observers note that of course, Graham himself had been one of the candidates in that bitter contest. Insults like “lightweight” and “jackass” were tossed back and forth, and Trump publicly shared Graham’s cellphone number. (Trump finally apologized for that stunt — at Graham’s funeral this past July. Better late than never, I suppose.).

By the time of Graham’s death this year, though, his earlier self would not have recognized the senator from South Carolina who had transformed himself into one of the president’s golfing buddies and closest allies.

It has been revealed that in May of this year, after Sen. Bill Cassidy lost his Louisiana primary to a Trump-backed opponent, Graham reasoned on NBC News that Cassidy lost because he “tried to destroy” the president, and warned the same fate would befall any Republican who crossed Trump. “This is the party of Donald Trump.”.

Why the switch? “He allowed me into his world. That’s great,” he told The Upcoming York Times.

Lindsey Graham stayed relevant, with a desired seat at the table — at a cost to his political reputation and legacy.

It has been revealed that after he died, Graham’s sister was appointed to complete his Senate term and was then pushed to run for a full term by her brother’s onetime nemesis Donald Trump. The president’s endorsement pushed Darline Graham past a more experienced Republican, Rep. Ralph Norman, in the Senate primary.

That she played a part in the Republicans’ historic midterm loss is a full-circle moment that Shakespeare would relish.

Graham lost to Dr. Annie Andrews, as the state elected a Democratic senator for the first time in decades. It came as a big surprise, especially to those Republicans who, like Lindsey Graham, started out as skeptics of the inexperienced, cruel president before making peace with the man, his policies and his power.

MAGA swallowed the GOP, and voters who elected Trump in 2016 and 2024 followed.

What was the breaking point for the people who ignored millions of dollars in attack ads on their way to the polls?

In Ohio, was it the Vivek Ramaswamy ad that dredged up opponent Amy Acton’s childhood trauma, supported by Trump and Vice President JD Vance?

In the South, was it the seeming glee of Republican state legislatures as they gerrymandered districts with substantial African American constituencies, all with the blessing of a Supreme Court-weakened Voting Rights Act?

In Texas, did Hispanic voters who swung to Trump in 2024 realize that ICE’s definition of “the worst of the worst” included business owners, grandmoms and schoolchildren?

Did tariffs turn off farmers as it affected expenses and bottom lines?

Did Americans rebel when they saw their dollars buy less while the president gushed over gold trinkets, a ballroom and a reflecting pool his hand-picked contractors couldn’t fix, and made billions for himself and his family?

Did the Islamophobia and anti-Semitism, the racism and homophobia in the name of Jesus leave true people of faith or just plain decent people disgusted?

In South Carolina, Darline Graham didn’t explain her looks for the economy or for fighting corruption or foreign entanglements, except to say “national security is not my thing” on a debate stage.

But the candidate with a scant resume did manage at a South Carolina rally to call her opponent “bats — crazy” while standing next to an approving Trump, who coined his own anti-trans slur for Andrews.

According to recent reports, andrews responded by saying: “If name-calling would help lower gas prices and grocery prices, he can call me all the names he wants. But I don’t think that’s going to get the job done.” In a state with 14 counties “without a single OB/Gyn,” as Andrews has remarked, the emptiness of insults is hard to miss.

Whatever lessons they draw from Tuesday, Democrats should not get comfortable.

Angry, hurting voters expect results — fast.

But for now, it’s hard not to recall the warning issued and then forgotten 10 years ago, with the hope that Republicans realize the old Lindsey might have been right all along.

This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.

The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just introduced a newly introduced cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.

Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.

In a recent development, in the first class of the day, baking novices and aficionados alike joined senior Test Kitchen editor and BA Bake Club expert Jesse Szewczyk in the Test Kitchen for Pie Crust Fundamentals, presented by East Fork. The hands-on class featured guest Keia Mastrianni, brand storyteller and “unofficial pie lady” of East Fork. Mastrianni proclaimed her enthusiasm for pie making: “I love preaching the gospel of pie. My favorite thing is teaching people to make pie dough with their hands.” Szewczyk agreed, emphasizing the tactile nature of the process: “It’s a very physical thing to do…a recipe can be written, but teaching someone to make pie dough requires demonstration.” Participants were in luck as Szewczyk and Mastrianni demonstrated a buttery pie crust fortified with cream cheese, a recipe ideal for Thanksgiving developed by former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic. After Mastrianni shared crimping tips, participants made their own pie dough at stations throughout the kitchen, with Test Kitchen editors on hand to offer guidance. One participant, James, was particularly excited to be working with director of cooking Emma Laperruque. He enthused, “Before Emma’s and Chris [Morocco’s] recipes, I would burn water. [Bon Appétit] has made cooking really accessible, and I built a lot of confidence. I love the simplicity of Emma’s recipes…they are all so flavorful and so good.”.

Industry observers note that each guest left ready for holiday baking season with fresh pie-making skills, and a ceramic pie dish from East Fork’s new bakeware collection, featuring clay and glaze made in-house with materials sourced in the Southeast. Before moving on to their next experience, Mastrianni encouraged everyone to keep honing their skills, emphasizing, “Practice makes pie. Progress, not perfection.”.

Meanwhile, in the neighboring Demo Kitchen, a Pasta Boot Camp was underway with Bon Appétit senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman and chef Stefano Secchi. Secchi, chef and partner of Upcoming York City’s Rezdôra (recipient of one Michelin star) and Massara, honed his craft in Modena, Italy, under legendary chef Massimo Bottura.

In a recent development, after walking guests through the fundamentals of making and shaping fresh pasta by hand, Secchi demonstrated a filled ravioli dish aptly named Holiday in Parma. Made with 00 flour and egg dough, the ravioli was piped with a chestnut and Parmesan filling and served with a rich reduction of chicken broth, butter, and saba (a traditional Italian syrup made from slowly simmered grape must).

While guests savored their pasta in the Demo Kitchen, a lively panel discussion was underway on the 34th floor. Moderated by editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, the Bringing Culture to Cooking panel featured chefs Fariyal Abdullahi (executive chef, Hav & Mar, NYC), Nicholas Bazik (chef and owner, Provenance, Philadelphia, a Bon Appétit Best Newly introduced Restaurant of 2025), and Vijay Kumar (executive chef and partner, Semma, NYC, a Best New Restaurant of 2022). The conversation explored how culture, identity, and personal experience inform each chef’s cooking. The chefs shared some of their favorite home-cooking ingredients, such as Chef Bazik’s fermented lime juice, a versatile seasoning made by combining fresh lime juice with salt at a 2% ratio by weight. Chef Abdullahi championed berbere, the Ethiopian spice blend she likened to “Ethiopian salt” for its ubiquity in the country’s cooking. Abdullahi cautioned that store-bought blends are convenient but not necessarily of the highest-possible quality. “You should make it at home!” she encouraged.

Back in the Test Kitchen, Visit Maine hosted Lobster 101, a hands-on lobster class and oyster tasting with Bon Appétit’s manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Each participant received a whole, steamed Maine lobster and the ingredients and tools needed to transform it into a creamy, decadent lobster dip. Under Westerfield’s guidance, the class learned how to break down their lobsters, extract the meat, and assemble a dip made with cream cheese, mayonnaise, celery, chives, and lemon juice. The approachable demonstration demystified the process and demonstrated guests how easily they could prepare a luxurious appetizer at home, just in time for the holidays.

Sources indicate that participants worked with hard-shell lobsters, but Tripp encouraged them to visit Maine and sample both hard-shell and soft-shell varieties. She explained that soft-shell lobsters, typically in season from July through August, have a sweeter, more tender meat. The two are actually the same animal at different stages of its molting cycle: a soft-shell lobster has recently shed its old shell, leaving a newer, more pliable one that is easier to crack. The class concluded with a tasting of Aphrodite Oysters, grown in the waters off South Thomaston, Maine. The medium-size oysters were briny and subtly sweet, reflecting the cold, brackish waters of the Lower Weskeag River where they were grown. A small squeeze of lemon was all that was needed to enhance their flavor as guests tilted their heads back, slurped, and allowed themselves to be transported to the rugged coast of Maine.

Meanwhile, in the Demo Kitchen, Bon Appétit director of culture Joseph Hernandez was joined by Matt Conroy, chef at Washington, DC’s Maison Bar à Vins, for a live cooking demonstration of one of Chef Conroy’s favorite dishes. Named one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026, the restaurant pairs French-inspired cooking with an eclectic wine list and seasonal cocktails. Chef Conroy prepared a new fall salad made of chicory, pear, and smoked blue cheese, finished with a Banyuls vinaigrette.

In the cafeteria, guests gathered for a live version of the Dear Bon Appétit advice column. Bon Appétit director of cooking Emma Laperruque presented questions about home cooking and holiday entertaining to chef Amanda Freitag. One attendee asked Freitag how to handle undercooked turkey legs and thighs each year. Freitag recommended removing the legs and cooking them separately, as in this BA recipe for Gravy-Braised Turkey from Jesse Szewczyk.

Next, food stylist Thu Buser showcased her exceptional culinary artistry by decorating an elaborate “snake cake” with vibrant green swirls and flowers. Then, a break for lunch with BA’s Best Mozzarella Sticks, a variety of salads and skewers, hot honey salmon, smoothies, and a cranberry maple mule.

While attendees grazed and mingled, Jamila Robinson joined legendary chef and restaurateur Marcus Samuelsson to discuss Back to Green: Rediscovering a World of Delicious, Healthy Eating, his upcoming global plant-forward cookbook coauthored by Robinson. Samuelsson captured the atmosphere of the event, remarking, “What a party we are having here…the energy is amazing!”.

Sources indicate that the final demonstration of the day featured Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote presented by Visit Maine with Jesse Szewczyk and Ron Howard of Brodis Blueberries. Featuring a recipe from Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firsker, the shortcakes showcased farm-fresh wild blueberries grown on a ninth-generation family farm. As Szewczyk prepared the recipe, Howard discussed the importance of wild blueberries to Maine’s agricultural heritage. A native crop, they can be traced back to the end of the last Ice Age, predating lobster as a symbol of the state. “Everyone should think of wild blueberries as the ultimate Maine crop,” Howard explained. After tasting the shortcakes, attendees would be hard-pressed to disagree. Szewczyk noted that compared with conventional blueberries, the wild blueberries produced a more saturated color and tasted more distinctly of blueberry.

The day ended on a sweet note with pastry chef Eunji Lee, winner of North America’s Best Pastry Chef Award from The 50. Attendees had a chance to meet Lee and sample pastries from Lysée, her pastry boutique influenced by Korean and French culture and inspired by Newly introduced York City.

Industry observers note that bon Appétit Live brought together chefs, culinary personalities, and food editors for a day of conversations, cooking, tasting, and learning. Attendees experienced the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen firsthand, learned directly from chefs and editors, and engaged with the people and products behind the food. As editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson noted, “Food is always an invitation…we are so happy to give everyone access to the same experiences we have.”.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Tech giant, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

The Best Subscription Boxes for Women: Sure to Wow the Women in Your Life

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tested by Katie Bandurski, Emily Way and Paul Rankin.
  • We've tested dozens of subscription services over the years, and these are our favorite subscription boxes for women.
  • Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tested by Katie Bandurski, Emily Way and Paul Rankin.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

We've tested dozens of subscription services over the years, and these are our favorite subscription boxes for women.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Recent findings suggest that we tested some of the best subscription boxes to find the ones truly worth gifting. Whether you’re shopping for a woman who has everything or treating yourself to something special, these thoughtfully curated subscriptions make it easy to discover upcoming favorites and enjoy a delightful surprise each month.

Looking for more inspiration? Explore our 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for gifts she’ll love.

BloomsyBox is your one-stop shop when it comes to flower and plant subsctiption boxes. The brand offers a variety of eco-friendly blooms spanning seasonal bouquets, roses, tropical flowers and even houseplants for gifting. Choose from classic arrangements, large, mixed bouquets or collections of roses in monthly, weekly or bi-weekly deliveries.

Madi Koetting for Taste of Home.

It has been revealed that “My BloomsyBox arrangement featuring red and white roses arrived expertly arranged, although I rapidly trimmed the stems for maximum freshness and plopped them in a clear glass vase,” says tester Madi Koetting. “Despite the less-than-ideal winter weather, my bouquet remained intact for a whopping two and a half weeks. BloomsyBox is another go-to for show-stopping flower delivery.”.

In a recent development, I re-tested BloomsyBox in 2026 to ensure quality and consistency. My Garden Soirée bouquet arrived via next-day delivery, with all 30 stems fresh and perfectly intact. BloomsyBox delivery is turly one of the freshest, fullest and most well-preserved flower delivery boxes I’ve ever received, and it would make a wonderful subscription gift for anyone who loves fresh blooms.

Sources indicate that A candle subscription that’s affordable, flexible and totally giftable may seem too good to be true, but we found an option that has it all. Vellabox offers flexible subscription options, and each candle comes from a different candlemaker, so there’s no limit to the number of scents and brands she’ll get to try. Plus, regardless of size, each box comes with a curated gift to accompany the candle.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Deputy Shopping Editor Katie Bandurski has been a Vellabox fan ever since trying them for her Vellabox review. She has received a number of candle companion gifts, from lip balms to an eco-friendly scrub brush. “I’ve received many Vellabox boxes over the years, and they’re all high quality. I’ve found so many amazing scents, and I love to give them as gifts,” she states.

Recent findings suggest that for the price point, we find Vellabox to be an incredible value for gifting, enjoying and exploring new scents. They’re also very well packaged to prevent breakage, and each comes in a pretty fabric pouch, sure to feel extra special to giftees.

In a recent development, our best chocolate box winner offers our favorite chocolate subscription box, too. I tested the Compartés Chocolate of the Month Club box in February—and it wowed from the moment it arrived. Inside were two chocolate bars and a box of assorted chocolates.

According to recent reports, the assortment featured strawberry cream and crème brûlée–filled chocolates. The strawberry cream was exactly what you’d expect—fruity and delicious. The crème brûlée, however, was a surprise, capturing the rich, warm vanilla flavor of the classic dessert with impressive accuracy.

February’s box included two chocolate bars: California Berries, a vegan dark chocolate full of dried berries, and Strawberry Shortcake, a white chocolate bar packed with strawberries and airy, crunchy shortcake pieces.

While the subscription does require a minimum of three deliveries (discounted to $180 from the $225 value), it would make a thoughtful gift, especially if you have a series of gifting occasions, like the holiday season aligning with someone’s birthday month.

After trying the most popular charcuterie clubs, we found that Appy Hour charcuterie kits offer a convenient, curated solution that takes the guesswork out of building a board—a perfect gift for casual hosts and aspiring entertainers alike.

An average subscription box from Appy Hour typically contains up to five cheeses, two meats, cracker packs and two or more accompaniments like dried fruits, olives, candied nuts, chocolate, spreads or pickled items. Tester Paul Rankin’s box included four packets of cured meats, three hard cheeses, one jar of sheep and goat cheese in oil, one sweet lemon ricotta, a box of artisan crisps, a bag of pralined pecans, a bag of dried cherries and, lastly, a tiny jar of blackberry balsamic jam.

“This entire box was exquisite,” indicates Paul. “I’m already a huge fan of a charcuterie board, so this was an easy winner. Each meat was different and delicious; the dried cherries and candied pecans tasted amazing. But the cheese, the cheese! The cheeses were the star, particularly the sweetened lemon ricotta, which was absolutely stunning.”.

The ease and quality of this kit are hard to beat, and buying each item separately would likely cost more than the price of the box, making it an excellent value for giving and receiving alike.

Sources indicate that if fruit is her snack of choice, The Fruit Company offers a wide selection of fresh fruit for delivery. There are multiple different monthly fruit clubs that include everything from pears and apples to more exotic choices like star fruit and champagne mangos. And you can choose different packaging options, from ribbons and bows to beautiful baskets.

“This is a solid fruit basket,” says Katie Bandurski of her Simply Organic Fruit Basket. “It’s beautifully arranged, shipped without any damage to the fruit and has a nice variety.”.

You can choose from four different subscription options: HarvestClub Americana (oranges, peaches, pineapples, cherries), HarvestClub Medley (a mix of hard-to-find fruits and familiar favorites, like Rainier cherries and Fuji apples), HarvestClub Organic (seasonal organic fruit) and HarvestClub Exotica (exotic fruit, like champagne mangos and star fruit). All boxes ship free and are available on 3-, 6- and 12-month-long options.

It has been revealed that looking for the perfect gift for an experienced baker? Crumble Crate offers monthly boxes that include pre-portioned dry ingredients, a recipe, at least one quality baking tool and a QR code that leads to instructional videos, shopping lists and extra tips.

According to recent reports, katie Bandurski tested the apple rose tart, which arrived with a tart pan and pastry cutter, along with specialty ingredients like almond flour. Some basics, including apples, butter, eggs and lemon juice, needed to be supplied separately.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Sources indicate that even as an experienced baker, Katie found the project challenging. Forming the apple roses took some patience, and she had to reread a few of the more involved steps. Still, the finished tart looked impressive and tasted excellent. She described the experience as equal parts baking project and art project.

Crumble Crate may be frustrating for a true beginner, but if you’re gifting to a baker who already knows her way around the kitchen, it makes every delivery feel like a worthwhile challenge.

Winc is one of the best-rated wine clubs out there, and the subscription wine club includes diverse selections with a little bit of everything, from sake to rosé.

You can select individual wines or fill out a survey to have bottles specially curated for you. While it doesn’t come with tasting notes or other supplemental information in the box, all of that is easily available on their website.

It has been revealed that tea Runners is a top pick when it comes to tea subscriptions. Each box includes four sampler pouches of tea, 10 tea bags and a postcard with some basic info about the club, tea origins and steeping instructions.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

According to recent reports, the Original Box is a great gift for her to start experimenting and figuring out what types of tea she likes. If she already knows what kind of tea she likes, she can choose from four box options: Black, Pure, Herbal or Original.

Inside Katie’s box, each tea impressed with its freshness and flavor. She likens Moonlight Jasmine to “a warm summer night,” whereas Floral Nectar Black wowed with its subtle finishing florals. Even the Majestic Earl Grey impressed Katie, who isn’t a significant fan of Earl Grey. “It was so delicious—much fresher than any Earl Grey I’ve had before,” she claims.

We adore Jeni’s ice cream, and our rave review of Jeni’s Pint of the Month Club may just convince you that this is the food subscription box you need to get her.

Industry observers note that katie claims, “I was impressed with the wide array of flavors in my ice cream subscription box. The mix had a little bit of everything—chocolaty, fruity, salty and even savory. Plus, many of these were flavors I would not have picked out myself. Talk about a great way to widen your ice cream palate!”.

Katie Bandurski For Taste of Home.

This one is definitely on the pricier side, but our editors absolutely love it.

The Partners Coffee Roaster’s choice subscription is one of the best ways to stay on top of the latest coffee. I tried Partners for the first time this year, and was blown away by the fresh, delicious flavor and quality of the brand’s whole bean coffee. The beans truly took my home latte to another level. Katie, who has also tried the brand, loves Partners for their bold packaging and both New York- and global-themed brews.

Katie Bandurski for Taste of Home.

It has been revealed that each 12-ounce bag is hand-selected by a member of the Partners team. You’ll receive both single-origin beans and blends, depending on the month. Enjoy delivery every one, two, three or four weeks, starting at $20 a bag. As an added bonus, you get free shipping with the coffee subscription.

Let’s just say, I have Partner’s Coffee on my personal Christmas list this year, and I’m hoping Santa comes through!

It has been revealed that any bookworm will appreciate this curated book box. Choose between a 3-, 6- and 12-month subscription, and your giftee will receive a specialty-bound read each month for the duration of the subscription.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Plus, Book of the Month is totally customizable. They’ll get to choose one book out of a selection of five or six books each month, and can even skip a month if they need some more time to read their last pick.

Industry observers note that I needed a gift for the family member who ‘has everything’ and also loves books—and BOTM was the perfect find. With BOTM, she can choose books she doesn’t already own from a curated list. Buying a subscription as a gift is super easy too. I opted for a physical card, which I tucked in a little gift basket with other goodies.

According to recent reports, jiggy is a puzzle company that focuses on partnering with artists through the Jiggy Puzzle Club. Members get an exclusive 500-piece puzzle each month, plus VIP perks like early access to new products and opportunities to interact with Jiggy artists. Each puzzle also comes with a reusable drawstring bag, making it highly giftable.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Industry observers note that to find the best subscription boxes for women, we drew on our extensive hands-on experience testing gift clubs and subscription services. While evaluating products for other guides, we compiled our top picks to help inform this roundup. Our team of expert editors and product testers tried and evaluated each option in their own homes and kitchens, taking detailed notes on the following factors:.

At Taste of Home, we’ve tested countless food and drink subscriptions for guides covering everything from the best food subscription boxes and gifts of the month clubs to fruit subscriptions and chocolate boxes. For this piece, we tapped into that extensive hands-on experience and our expertise in testing and evaluating a wide range of subscription services to find the best subscriptions to gift to women.

According to recent reports, not only is this an incredibly delicious, cheese-stuffed, light-as-air way to start the day, but it also gives your protein goals a kickstart to fuel you through the morning. It also whips up in a blender in seconds, making it the perfect easy, make-ahead breakfast you need before a busy week.

Recent findings suggest that slow-cooked turkey legs are this year’s ultimate Thanksgiving hack. No basting, no inevitable dry meat—no fuss at all. All you have to do is make an easy festive herb butter, wrap everything in foil, and let it roast unsupervised.

Industry observers note that green beans deserve to have a friend in the classic casserole, and by friend, we mean bacon. This mashup dish takes its cue from loaded baked potatoes and adds bacon, chives, and SO much cheese (just the right amount) for the perfect upgraded side.

Industry observers note that think your Hamburger Helper isn’t helpful enough? Add more protein! Recent findings suggest that these truffles are for those who love pecan pie but always ask for “just a sliver” at the holiday table. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, even Ina isn't making everything from scratch this year.
  • Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature.
  • Recent findings suggest that ina Garten has made her position on Thanksgiving dinner quite clear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

According to recent reports, even Ina isn't making everything from scratch this year. Her newly revealed side dishes include some surprisingly simple shortcuts.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Recent findings suggest that ina Garten has made her position on Thanksgiving dinner quite clear. The turkey may be the centerpiece, but the side dishes are the real stars. “Thanksgiving is one of those meals where I care more about the sides than the main event!” she recently shared with her followers.

In a recent Instagram post, Ina revealed that she’s especially excited to make several upcoming dishes from her latest cookbook, Simply Ina. There are familiar Thanksgiving favorites with a few clever twists, along with some store-bought shortcuts that prove even the Barefoot Contessa knows when to let someone else do part of the work. It’s a reassuring approach to a meal that can demand a lot of time in the kitchen.

Here’s a look at the six recipes Ina shared, along with similar Taste of Home dishes you can make for your own Thanksgiving dinner.

Ina’s combination of caramelized butternut squash and dried cranberries makes particularly good sense for Thanksgiving. Roasting brings out the squash’s natural sweetness, while the tart cranberries provide some welcome contrast. It’s a colorful alternative to the sweeter squash dishes that tend to find their way onto holiday tables, but one that wouldn’t look out of place next to a generous helping of Ina’s sausage and herb stuffing.

Try a Taste of Home version: Butternut Squash Jumble.

Ina has always been a champion of making Thanksgiving easier, and her fresh turkey gravy takes that philosophy a step further. She’s starting with canned turkey gravy, then dressing it up for a richer, more homemade flavor. It’s a practical shortcut for someone who’s spent years teaching us how to make gravy from scratch. And as Ina points out, nobody wants leftover turkey without gravy, either. Making enough for Friday’s sandwiches is simply good planning.

Try a Taste of Home version: Make-Ahead Turkey Gravy.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Sources indicate that mashed potatoes are practically guaranteed a place on the Thanksgiving table, but Ina’s addition of garlic gives this familiar favorite a welcome savory kick. Ina actually starts with Bob Evans prepared mashed potatoes, then dresses them up with garlic confit, butter and half-and-half. With so many sweet, rich dishes competing for space on the plate, garlic mashed potatoes offer a little balance without sacrificing any of the buttery comfort everyone expects.

Try a Taste of Home version: Garlic Mashed Potatoes.

Sources indicate that brussels sprouts have come a long way from the boiled vegetables many of us remember from childhood, and Ina’s version pairs them with pecorino, a salty, sharp sheep’s milk cheese. The combination makes sense: The cheese adds richness and a savory bite that complements the sprouts’ slightly bitter flavor. It’s the sort of side dish that might even persuade a few longtime Brussels sprouts skeptics to reconsider.

Try a Taste of Home version: Brussels Sprouts with Garlic & Goat Cheese.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, here’s where Ina’s fondness for a good shortcut really comes into play. Her Chunky Cranberry Conserve starts with canned whole-berry cranberry sauce, which she dresses up with grated Granny Smith apple, orange juice and zest, raisins and pecans. The result has more texture and complexity than the contents of the can alone, without requiring you to start from scratch.

According to recent reports, there’s something reassuring in knowing Ina Garten is perfectly content to open a can of cranberry sauce on Thanksgiving. If it’s good enough for Ina, the rest of us can probably stop apologizing for it.

Try a Taste of Home version: Cranberry-Apple Chutney.

Sources indicate that sweet potatoes are a Thanksgiving staple, but Ina’s combination of maple syrup and chipotle gives them a welcome change of direction. The maple enhances their natural sweetness, while the smoky heat of chipotle keeps the dish firmly on the savory side of dinner.

And there’s another shortcut hiding in this dish. In a recent interview with Cup of Jo, Ina revealed that she uses prepared mashed sweet potatoes from Trader Joe’s, adding chipotle powder, maple syrup, butter and seasonings to make them her own. She figures nobody would know she hadn’t roasted the sweet potatoes herself, and with everything else that needs cooking on Thanksgiving, that’s a shortcut (and a great Trader Joe’s find) worth stealing.

Try a Taste of Home version: Hot Honey Sweet Potatoes.

31 Cranberry Recipes for Thanksgiving and Beyond
